# Reaction Feasibility ## Feasible Reactions > **Spec point** — `spcpt_b5Tc4T4s2vBZNy4r` ## Reaction Feasibility - The Gibbs equation can be used to calculate whether a reaction is **feasible **or not **Δ*****G*****θ**** = Δ*****H******reaction*****θ**** - TΔ*****S******system*****θ** - When Δ*G*θ is **negative**, the reaction is **feasible **and likely to occur - When Δ*G*θ is **positive**, the reaction is **not feasible** and unlikely to occur > **Worked Example** > Calculate the Gibbs free energy for the following reaction at 298 K and determine whether the reaction is feasible. > > 2Ca (s) + O2 (g) → 2CaO (s) Δ*H*θ = -635.5 kJ mol-1 > > - *S*θ[Ca (s)] = 41.00 J K-1 mol-1 > - *S*θ[O2 (s)] = 205.0 J K-1 mol-1 > - *S*θ[CaO (s)] = 40.00 J K-1 mol-1 > > **Answer:** > > - **Step 1: **Calculate Δ*S*systemθ > > Δ*S**system*θ = ΣΔ*S**products*θ - ΣΔ*S**reactants*θ > > Δ*S**system*θ = (2 x Δ*S*θ [CaO(s)]) - (2 x Δ*S*θ [Ca(s)] + Δ*S**θ* [O2(g)]) > > Δ*S**system*θ = (2 x 40.00) - (2 x 41.00 + 205.0) > > Δ*S**system*θ = -207.0 J K-1 mol-1 > > - **Step 2: **Convert Δ*S*θ to kJ K-1 mol-1 > > Δ*S*θ = $\frac{-207.0}{1000}$ = -0.207 kJ K-1 mol-1 > > - **Step 3: **Calculate Δ*G*θ > > Δ*G*θ = Δ*H**reaction*θ - TΔ*S**system*θ > > Δ*G*θ = -635.5 - (298 x -0.207) > > Δ*G*θ = -573.8 kJ mol-1 > > - **Step 4: **Determine whether the reaction is feasible > > - Since the Δ*G*θ*** ***is **negative **the reaction is feasible and likely to occur ## Reaction Feasibility & Temperature Changes > **Spec point** — `spcpt_H85BWCdQWKcQkjZJ` ## Reaction Feasibility & Temperature Changes - The **feasibility **of a reaction can be affected by the **temperature** - The Gibbs equation will be used to explain what will affect the feasibility of a reaction for exothermic and endothermic reactions ![Entropy - Gibbs Equation, downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/79edb59f3b46-5-2-entropy-gibbs-equation.png) ### Exothermic reactions - In exothermic reactions, Δ*H**reaction*θ** **is **negative** - If the Δ*S**system*θ is **positive:** - Both the first and second term will be **negative** - Resulting in a **negative** Δ*G*θ so the reaction is **feasible** - Therefore, regardless of the temperature, an exothermic reaction with a positive Δ*S**system*θ will **always be feasible** - If the Δ*S**system*θ is **negative:** - The first term is **negative **and the second term is **positive** - At high temperatures, the -*T*Δ*S**system*θ will be very **large** and **positive** and will overcome Δ*H**reaction*θ - Therefore, at **high temperatures** Δ*G*θ is **positive** and the reaction is not feasible - The reaction is more **feasible** at low temperatures, as the second term will not be large enough to overcome Δ*H**reaction*θ resulting in a negative Δ*G*θ - This corresponds to Le Chatelier’s principle which states that for **exothermic reactions **an increase in temperature will cause the equilibrium to shift position in favour of the reactants, i.e. in the endothermic direction - In other words, for exothermic reactions, the products will **not be formed **at high temperatures - The reaction is **not feasible **at high temperatures #### Summary of factors affecting Gibbs free energy for exothermic reactions | **If Δ*****H ....*** | **And if Δ*****S***** ....** | **Then Δ*****G is*** | **Spontaneous? ** | **Because** | |---|---|---|---|---| | is negative

# Electrolysis: Calculations

## Electrolysis Calculations

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_KDKVs5TNM2f5ZT22`

## Electrolysis Calculations

- **Faraday’s constant **can be used to calculate:

  - The **mass** of a substance **deposited** at an electrode
  - The **volume **of gas **liberated **at an electrode

### Calculating the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode

- To calculate the mass of a substance deposited at the electrode, you need to be able to:

  - Write the half-equation at the electrode
  - Determine the number of coulombs needed to form one mole of substance at the specific electrode using Faraday’s constant
  - Calculate the charge transferred during electrolysis
  - Use simple proportion and the relative atomic mass of the substance to find its mass

> **Worked Example**
> Calculate the amount of magnesium deposited when a current of 2.20 A flows through the molten bromide for 15 minutes.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> - The magnesium (Mg<sup>2+</sup>) ion is a positively charged cation that will move towards the cathode.
> - **Step 1: **Write the half-equation at the cathode
> 
> **Mg**<sup>**2+**</sup>**(aq)          +          2e**<sup>**-**</sup>**       →         Mg(s)**
> 
> **1 mol                           2 mol               1 mol**
> 
> - **Step 2:** Determine the number of coulombs required to deposit one mole of magnesium at the cathode
> 
> For every one mole of electrons, the number of coulombs needed is 96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> In this case, there are **two moles** of electrons required
> 
> So, the number of coulombs needed is:
> 
> *F* = 2 x 96 500
> 
> *F* = 193 000 C mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> - **Step 3: **Calculate the charge transferred during the electrolysis
> 
> *Q* = I x t
> 
> Q = 2.20 x (60 x 15) = 1980 C** **
> 
> - **Step 4: **Calculate the mass of magnesium deposited by simple proportion using the relative atomic mass of Mg
> 
> | **Charge (C)** | **Amount of Mg deposited (mol)** | **Amount of Mg deposited (g)** |
> |---|---|---|
> | 193 000 | 1 | 24.3 |
> | 1980 | $\frac{1980}{193000}$ = 0.0103 | 0.0103 x 24.3 = 0.25 |
> 
> - Therefore, 0.25 g of magnesium is deposited at the cathode

### Calculating the volume of gas liberated at an electrode

- To calculate the volume of gas liberated at an electrode, you need to be able to:

  - Write the half-equation at the electrode
  - Determine the number of coulombs needed to form one mole of substance at the specific electrode using Faraday’s constant
  - Calculate the charge transferred during electrolysis
  - Use simple proportion and the relationship 1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> at room temperature

> **Worked Example**
> Calculate the volume of **oxygen** gas produced at room temperature, when a concentrated aqueous solution of sulfuric acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, is electrolysed for 35.0 minutes using a current of 0.75 A.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> - The oxygen gas is formed from the **oxidation **of negatively charged hydroxide (OH<sup>-</sup>) ions at the anode-
> - **Step 1: **Write the half-equation at the anode
> 
> **   4**OH<sup>- </sup>(aq)         →         O<sub>2 </sub>(g)               +          **2**H<sub>2</sub>O (l)            +          4e<sup>-</sup>
> 
> 4 mol                           1 mol                           2 mol                           4 mol
> 
> - **Step 2: **Determine the number of coulombs required to form one mole of oxygen gas at the anode
> 
> For every one mole of electrons, the number of coulombs needed is 96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> So, for **four moles** of electrons, the number of coulombs needed is:
> 
> *F* = 4 x 96 500
> 
> *F* = 386 000 C mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> - **Step 3: **Calculate the charge transferred during the electrolysis
> 
> *Q* = I x t
> 
> Q = 0.75 x (60 x 35) = 1575 C
> 
> - **Step 4: **Calculate the volume of oxygen liberated by simple proportion using the relationship 1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> at room temperature
> 
> | **Charge (C)** | **Amount of O**<sub>**2**</sub>** liberated (mol)** | **Amount of O**<sub>**2**</sub>** liberated (dm**<sup>**3**</sup>**)** |
> |---|---|---|
> | 386 000 | 1 | 24 |
> | 1575 | $\frac{1575}{386000}$ = 4.080 x 10<sup>-3</sup> | 4.080 x 10<sup>-3 </sup>x 24.0 = 0.0979 |
> 
> - Therefore, 0.0979 dm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen is formed at the anode

> **Worked Example**
> Calculating the volume of **hydrogen** gas produced at room temperature, when a concentrated aqueous solution of sodium sulfate, Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, is electrolysed for 17.5 minutes using a current of 3.25 A.
> 
> The hydrogen gas is formed from the **reduction** of positively charged hydrogen ions, H<sup>+</sup> at the cathode.
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Write the half-equation at the cathode
> 
> **2H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq)   +     2e**<sup>**-**</sup>**       →         H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)              **
> 
> **2 mols             2 mols             1 mol   **
> 
> - **Step 2: **Determine the number of coulombs required to form one mole of hydrogen gas at the cathode
> 
>   - For every one mole of electrons, the number of coulombs needed is:
> 
> *F* = 96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> *F* = 1 x 96 500
> 
> *F* = 96 500 C
> 
> - So, for **two moles** of electrons, the number of coulombs needed is:
> 
> *F* = 2 x 96 500
> 
> *F* = 193 000 C
> 
> - **Step 3: **Calculate the charge transferred during the electrolysis
> 
> *Q* = I x t
> 
> Q = 3.25 x (60 x 17.5) = 3 413 C
> 
> - **Step 4: **Calculate the volume of hydrogen liberated by simple proportion using the relationship 1 mol of gas occupies 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> at room temperature
> 
> | **Charge (C)** | **Amount of H**<sub>**2**</sub>** liberated (mol)** | **Amount of H**<sub>**2**</sub>** liberated (dm**<sup>**3**</sup>**)** |
> |---|---|---|
> | 193 000 | 1 | 24 |
> | 3413 | $\frac{3413}{193000}$ = 1.76 x 10<sup>-2</sup> | 1.76 x 10<sup>-2 </sup>x 24 = 0.42 |
> 
> - Therefore, 0.42 dm<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen is formed at the cathode

# Electrolysis

## Products of Electrolysis

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_m3t673F5zKPpKkb6`

## Products of Electrolysis

- **Electrolysis **is the breaking down of a compound into its elements using an **electric current**
- For example, the electrolysis of zinc chloride (ZnCl<sub>2</sub>) into its elements zinc and chlorine

**ZnCl**<sub>**2**</sub>** → Zn + Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** **

- This method is often used to:

  - Extract **metals **from their **metal ores** when the metals cannot be extracted by heating their ores with carbon
  - Purify metals
  - Produce non-metals such as fluorine
- Electrolysis is carried out in an electrolysis cell which consists of:

  - An **electrolyte** - this is the compound that is broken down during electrolysis and it is either a **molten ionic compound **or a **concentrated aqueous solution of ions**
  - Two **electrodes** - these are metal or graphite rods conduct electricity to the electrolyte and away from the electrolyte
  
    - The positive electrode is called the **anode**
    - The negative electrode is called the **cathode**
  - The power supply, which is **direct current**

#### An electrochemical cell

![Principles of Electrochemistry - Basics of electrolysis, downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/9fa48bf93c8f-5-3-principles-of-electrochemistry-basics-of-ele.png)

***Electrolysis takes place in an electrochemical cell; this type of electrochemical cell is called an electrolytic cell***

### Electrolysis of molten electrolytes

- **Cations **(positively charged ions) move to the **negatively charged cathode** where they **gain electrons**

  - **Reduction** takes place at the cathode
  - If a **metal** is formed, a layer of metal is deposited on a cathode or it forms a **molten layer** in the cell
  - If **hydrogen** gas is formed, bubbles are seen
  - For example, silver and hydrogen both form positively charged ions which would be **reduced **at the cathode as follows:

**Ag**<sup>**+**</sup>** + e**<sup>**-**</sup>** → Ag**

**2H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**+ 2e**<sup>**-**</sup>** → H**<sub>**2**</sub>

- **Anions **(negatively charged ions) move to the **positively charged** **anode** where they **lose electrons**

  - **Oxidation** takes place at the anode
  - For example, bromine forms negatively charged ions which would be **oxidised **at the anode as follows:

**2Br**<sup>**-**</sup>** → Br**<sub>**2**</sub>** + 2e**<sup>**-**</sup>

#### Products formed by electrolysis when a pure molten ionic compound containing two simple ions is electrolysed

- Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>

  - Cathode = Al
  - Anode = O<sub>2</sub>
- MgBr<sub>2</sub>

  - Cathode = Mg
  - Anode = Br<sub>2</sub>
- NaCl

  - Cathode = Na
  - Anode = Cl<sub>2</sub>
- ZnI<sub>2</sub>

  - Cathode =Zn
  - Anode = I<sub>2</sub>

### Electrolysis of aqueous solutions

- **Aqueous** **solutions** have more than one cation and anion in solution due to the presence of **water**
- Water contributes H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>- </sup>ions to the solution, which makes things more complicated

  - Water is a weak electrolyte and splits into H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>-</sup> ions as follows:

**H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O ⇌ H**<sup>**+**</sup>** + OH**<sup>**-**</sup>

- The actual ions that are **discharged** during electrolysis will depend on:

  - The relative electrode potential of the ions
  - The concentration of the ions

### Relative electrode potential of ions

- The **relative electrode potential **(*E*<sup>**θ**</sup>) of ions describes how easily an ion is discharged during electrolysis
- The **positively charged** **cation** with the most **positive** *E*<sup>θ</sup> will be discharged at the **cathode** as this is the cation that is most easily **reduced**

  - For example, a concentrated **aqueous solution** of NaF will contain hydrogen (H<sup>+</sup>) and sodium (Na<sup>+</sup>) ions
  - The half-equations for the reduction of these ions and their *E*<sup>θ</sup> values are as follows:

**2H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**-  **</sup>**⇌ H**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g)     *****E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** *****=  *****0.00 V**

**Na**<sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) + e**<sup>**-  **</sup>**⇌ Na (s)     *****E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** *****= *****-2.71 V**

- Since H<sup>+ </sup>ions have a higher *E*<sup>θ</sup> value, hydrogen gas (H<sub>2</sub>) is formed at the **cathode **instead of sodium (Na)
- The negatively charged anion that is **most easily oxidised** will be discharged at the **anode**
- This corresponds to the half-reaction with the **least positive** (or most negative) *E*<sup>θ</sup>

  - For example, a concentrated aqueous solution of NaF will contain hydroxide (OH⁻) and fluoride (F⁻) ions
  - The half-equations for the reduction of the products and their *E*<sup>θ</sup> values are as follows (this is the standard way they are shown in data booklets):

** O**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) + 2H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) + 4e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ 4OH**<sup>**- **</sup>**(aq) **<sup>**         **</sup>***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** *****= *****+0.40 V**

** F**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ 2F**<sup>**- **</sup>**(aq) **<sup>**      **</sup>***E***<sup>**θ **</sup>***= *****+2.87 V**

- Since the OH<sup>-</sup>/O<sub>2</sub> half-reaction has a **less positive *****E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** value** (+0.40 V) than the F⁻/F<sub>2</sub> half-reaction (+2.87 V), hydroxide ions are **more easily oxidised** than fluoride ions

  - Therefore, **oxygen (O**<sub>**2**</sub>**) gas is formed at the anode**

### Concentration of ions

- Ions that are present in **higher** **concentrations** are more likely to be discharged
- For example, when a **concentrated **solution of NaF is electrolysed, there are far more **fluoride **ions which are discharged at the anode, instead of the **hydroxide** ions as the fluoride ions are in higher concentration

  - So, mainly fluorine will form at the electrode
- However, if a **very** **dilute** solution of NaF is electrolysed, there will be much more **oxygen** and much less fluorine gas formed at the anode

  - In reality, a mixture of both oxygen and fluorine gas is formed

> **Exam Hint**
> Electrolysis is a redox reaction as a reduction reaction takes place at one electrode and an oxidation reaction at the other electrode
> 
> When writing the overall redox equation make sure that the electrons lost at the anode balance the electrons gained at the cathode
> 
> For example:
> 
> - Cathode: Cu<sup>2+ </sup>+ 2e<sup>-</sup> → Cu
> - Anode: 2Cl<sup>- </sup>→ Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>
> - Overall: CuCl<sub>2</sub> → Cu + Cl<sub>2</sub>

# Faraday's Law & Avogadro

## Faraday's Law

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_5Htx34tTFk52Gr3T`

## Faraday's Law

- The **amount** of substance that is formed at an electrode during **electrolysis** is proportional to:

  - The amount of **time** where a constant current to passes
  - The **amount** **of** **charge**, in coulombs, that passes through the electrolyte (strength of electric **current**)
  - The relationship between the current and time is:

***Q = I x t***

- **Q** = charge (coulombs, C)

  - **I** = current (amperes, A)
  - **t **= time, (seconds, s)
- The **amount **or the **quantity of electricity **can also be expressed by the **faraday** **(*****F*****) **unit

  - One faraday is the amount of **electric charge **carried by 1 mole of electrons or 1 mole of singly charged ions
  - 1 faraday is 96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - Thus, the relationship between the Faraday constant and the Avogadro constant (*L*) is:

***F = L x e***

- **F** = Faraday’s constant (96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>)

  - **L** = Avogadro’s constant (6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>)
  - **e** = charge on an electron

> **Worked Example**
> Determine the amount of electricity required for the following reactions:
> 
> 1) To deposit 1 mol of sodium
> 
> Na<sup>+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> → Na (s)
> 
> 2) To deposit 1 mol of magnesium
> 
> Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Mg (s)
> 
> 3) To form 1 mol of fluorine gas
> 
> 2F<sup>–</sup> (aq)  → F<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2e<sup>–</sup>
> 
> 4) To form 1 mole of oxygen
> 
> 4OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)  → O<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) +  4e<sup>–</sup>
> 
> **Answers:**
> 
> - One Faraday is the amount of charge (96 500 C) carried by 1 mole of electrons
> 
> **Answer 1:**
> 
> - As there is one mole of electrons, one faraday of electricity (96 500 C) is needed to deposit one mole of sodium.
> 
> **Answer 2:**
> 
> - Now, there are two moles of electrons, therefore, two faradays of electricity (2 x 96 500 C) are required to deposit one mole of magnesium.
> 
> **Answer 3:**
> 
> - Two moles of electrons are released, so it requires two faradays of electricity (2 x 96 500 C) to form one mole of fluorine gas.
> 
> **Answer 4:**
> 
> - Four moles of electrons are released, therefore it requires four faradays of electricity (4 x 96 500 C) to form one mole of oxygen gas.

## Determining Avogadro's Constant by Electrolysis

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_gPKQX6szPddTgJ9j`

## Determining Avogadro's Constant by Electrolysis

- The Avogadro’s constant (*L*) is the number of entities in **one mole**

  - *L* = 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>
  - For example, **four moles **of water contains 2.41 x 10<sup>24</sup> (6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> x 4) molecules of H<sub>2</sub>O
- The value of *L* (6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>) can be **experimentally **determined by electrolysis using the following equation:

***L *****=** $\frac{charge on1molofelectrons}{charge on1electron}$

### Finding L experimentally

- The charge on **one mole of electrons **is found by using a simple **electrolysis** experiment using copper electrodes

#### Apparatus set-up for finding the value of L experimentally

![Diagram of an electrolytic cell with copper anode and cathode in copper(II) sulphate solution, connected to direct current through an ammeter and variable resistor.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/37a796d05191-21455-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-3-p.png)

*Electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate solution*

- **Method**

  - The pure copper** anode **and pure copper** cathode **are **weighed**
  - A **variable** **resistor** is kept at a constant current of about 0.17 A
  - An **electric** **current** is then passed through for a certain time interval (e.g. 40 minutes)
  - The anode and cathode are then removed, washed with distilled water, dried with propanone, and then **reweighed**
- **Results**

  - The **cathode** has **increased** in mass as copper is deposited
  - The **anode** has **decreased** in mass as the copper goes into solution as copper ions
  - Often, it is the decreased mass of the anode which is used in the calculation, as the solid copper formed at the cathode does not always stick to the cathode properly
  - Let’s say the amount of copper deposited in this experiment was 0.13 g
- **Calculation:**

  - The amount of charge passed can be calculated as follows:

**Q = I x t**

**= 0.17 x (60 x 40)**

**= 408 C**

- To deposit 0.13 g of copper (2.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol), 408 C of electricity was needed
- The amount of electricity needed to deposit 1 mole of copper can therefore be calculated using simple proportion using the relative atomic mass of Cu

#### Calculating the amount of charge required to deposit one mole of copper table

- To scale our experimental results up to the molar level, we can use a ratio method
- The scaling factor tells us how many times larger our target amount (1 mole) is compared to our experimental result.

| **Charge (C)** | **Scaling factor** | **Amount of Cu deposited (g)** |
|---|---|---|
| 408 | $\frac{63.5}{0.13}$ = 488.5 | 0.13 |
| $\frac{63.5}{0.13}\times408=199,292$ | 1 (the target is 488.5 times bigger | 63.5 |

- Therefore, 199 292 C of electricity is needed to deposit 1 mole of Cu
- The half-equation shows that **2 mol of electrons **are needed to deposit one mol of copper:

**Cu**<sup>**2+ **</sup>**(aq) +  2e**<sup>**-**</sup>** →   Cu (s)**

- So, the charge on **1 mol** of electrons is:

  - Q = $\frac{199292}{2}=99646C$
- Given that the charge on **one electron** is 1.60 x 10<sup>-19</sup> C, then *L* equals:

  - *L* = $\frac{\mathrm{charge} \mathrm{on}1\mathrm{mol} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{electrons}}{\mathrm{charge} \mathrm{on}1\mathrm{electron}}$
  - *L* = $\frac{99646}{1.60\times10^{-19}}$ = 6.23 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

- The **experimentally** **determined** value for *L* of 6.23 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> is very close to the **theoretical **value of 6.02 x 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

# Measuring the Standard Electrode Potential

## Measuring the Standard Electrode Potential

> **Spec point** — `24.2.3`

## Measuring the Standard Electrode Potential

- There are three different types of half-cells that can be connected to a standard hydrogen electrode

  - A metal / metal ion half-cell
  - A non-metal / non-metal ion half-cell
  - An ion / ion half-cell (the ions are in different oxidation states)
- When a half-cell is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode, or when two half-cells are connected, a** salt bridge** is required

  - A salt bridge has **mobile ions** that complete the circuit
  - A salt bridge is typically a strip of filter paper soaked in a saturated solution of **potassium nitrate **or **potassium chloride **as nitrates and chlorides are usually soluble
  - This should ensure that no precipitates form which can affect the equilibrium position of the half-cells

### Metal / metal ion half-cell

- An example of a metal / metal ion half-cell is the Ag<sup>+</sup>/ Ag half-cell

  - Ag is the metal
  - Ag<sup>+</sup> is the metal ion
- This half-cell is connected to a **standard hydrogen electrode** and the two half-equations are:

**Ag**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Ag (s)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**= + 0.80 V**

**2H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**= 0.00 V **

- Since the Ag<sup>+</sup> / Ag half-cell has a more positive *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value, this is the **positive pole **and the H<sup>+</sup> / H<sub>2</sub> half-cell is the **negative** pole
- The **standard cell potential (***E*<sub>*cell*</sub><sup>ꝋ</sup>) is ***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = (+ 0.80) - (0.00) = + 0.80 V**
- The Ag<sup>+ </sup>ions are more likely to get **reduced **than the H<sup>+</sup> ions as it has a greater *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value

  - Reduction occurs at the **positive pole**
  - Oxidation occurs at the **negative pole**

#### Example of an electrochemical cell containing a metal / metal ion half-cell

![Diagram of an electrochemical cell with hydrogen gas, platinum wire, dilute acid, salt bridge, silver electrode, and high resistance voltmeter.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/013c826f6922-28069-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-3-p.png)

*Under standard conditions, a metal / metal ion half-cell is connected to the standard hydrogen electrode to measure the cell potential*

### Non-metal / non-metal ion half-cell

- In a **non-metal / non-metal ion **half-cell **platinum **wire or foil is used as an electrode to make electrical contact with the solution

  - Like graphite, platinum is inert and does not take part in the reaction
  - The redox equilibrium is established on the platinum surface
- An example of a non-metal/non-metal ion is the Br<sub>2</sub> / Br<sup>-</sup> half-cell

  - Br is the non-metal
  - Br<sup>-</sup> is the non-metal ion
- The half-cell is connected to a **standard hydrogen electrode** and the two half-equations are:

**Br**<sub>**2**</sub>** (l) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ 2Br**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +1.09 V**

**2H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = 0.00 V   **

- The Br<sub>2</sub> / Br<sup>-</sup> half-cell is the **positive pole** and the H<sup>+</sup> / H<sub>2</sub> is the **negative** pole
- ***E***<sub>**cell**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = (+ 1.09) - (0.00) = + 1.09 V**
- The Br<sub>2</sub> molecules are more likely to get **reduced **than H<sup>+</sup> as they have a greater *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value

#### Example of an electrochemical cell containing a non-metal / non-metal ion half-cell

![Diagram of a galvanic cell with hydrogen and bromine gas, platinum electrodes, a salt bridge, and a voltmeter showing 1.09 volts.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/14486f908d46-63417-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-3-p.png)

*Under standard conditions, a non-metal / non-metal ion half-cell is connected to the standard hydrogen electrode to measure the cell potential*

#### Ion / Ion half-cell

- A **platinum electrode **is again used to form a half-cell of ions that are in **different oxidation states**
- An example of such a half-cell is the MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> / Mn<sup>2+</sup> half-cell

  - MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> is an ion containing Mn with an oxidation number of +7
  - The Mn<sup>2+ </sup>ion contains Mn with an oxidation number of +2
- This half-cell is connected to a **standard hydrogen electrode** and the two half-equations are:

**MnO**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**-**</sup>** (aq) + 8H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + 5e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Mn**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 4H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)       *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +1.52 V**

**2H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)       *****E***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**= 0.00 V   **

- The H<sup>+</sup> ions are also present in the half-cell as they are required to convert MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>- </sup>into Mn<sup>2+ </sup>ions
- The MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> / Mn<sup>2+</sup> <sup>-</sup> half-cell is the **positive pole** and the H<sup>+</sup> / H<sub>2</sub> is the **negative** pole
- ***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = (+ 1.52) - (0.00) = + 1.52 V**

#### Example of an electrochemical cell containing an ion / ion half-cell

![Diagram of an electrochemical cell with hydrogen gas, platinum electrodes, sulphuric acid, salt bridge, manganese solutions, and voltmeter reading 1.52V.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/8e47d2f99d75-10376-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-3-p.png)

*Under standard conditions, an ion / ion half-cell is connected to the standard hydrogen electrode to measure the cell potential*

## Standard Cell Potential: Direction of Electron Flow & Feasibility

> **Spec point** — `24.2.5`

## Standard Cell Potential: Direction of Electron Flow & Feasibility

### Direction of electron flow

- The **direction of electron flow **can be determined by comparing the *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>values of two half-cells in an electrochemical cell

**Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ 2Cl**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +1.36 V**

**Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Cu (s)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +0.34 V**

- The Cl<sub>2</sub> more **readily accept** electrons from the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu half-cell

  - This is the **positive pole**
  - Cl<sub>2</sub> gets more readily reduced
- The Cu<sup>2+</sup> more **readily loses **electrons to the Cl<sub>2</sub>/Cl<sup>-</sup> half-cell

  - This is the **negative pole**
  - Cu<sup>2+ </sup>gets more readily oxidised
- The electrons flow from the Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu half-cell to the Cl<sub>2</sub>/Cl<sup>-</sup> half-cell
- The flow of electrons is from the **negative pole **to the **positive pole**

#### Flow of electrons through an electrochemical cell

![Diagram of an electrochemical cell with a voltmeter showing 1.02 V. It includes a salt bridge connecting Cu²⁺ and Cl⁻ solutions with electrodes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/d63f7a71a57e-3838-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021025-3-pr.png)

*The electrons flow through the wires from the negative pole to the positive pole*

### Feasibility

- The *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>values of a species indicate how **easily **they can get **oxidised **or **reduced**
- The **more **positive the value, the easier it is to reduce the species on the **left** of the half-equation

  - The reaction will tend to proceed in the **forward direction**
- The **less **positive the value, the easier it is to **oxidise** the species on the **right **of the half-equation

  - The reaction will tend to proceed in the backward direction
  - A reaction is **feasible **(likely to occur) when the *E*<sub>*cell*</sub><sup>ꝋ</sup> is **positive**
- For example, two half-cells in the following electrochemical cell are:

**Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ 2Cl**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +1.36 V**

**Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Cu (s)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +0.34 V**

- Cl<sub>2</sub> molecules are **reduced **as they have a more positive *E*<sup>ꝋ</sup> value
- The chemical reaction that occurs in this half-cell is:

**Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**→ 2Cl**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)          **

- Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions are **oxidised **as they have a less positive *E*<sup>ꝋ</sup> value
- The chemical reaction that occurs in this half-cell is:

**Cu (s) → Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**-**</sup>

- The **overall equation **of the electrochemical cell is (after cancelling out the electrons):

**Cu (s) + Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) → 2Cl**<sup>**- **</sup>**(aq) + Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)**

OR

**Cu (s) + Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) → CuCl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (s)**

- The **forward** reaction is **feasible** (spontaneous) as it has a **positive** *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup> value of +1.02 V ((+1.36) - (+0.34))
- The **backward **reaction is **not feasible** (not spontaneous) as it has a **negative** *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value of -1.02 ((+0.34) - (+1.36))

#### Reaction feasibility and the standard cell potential

![Principles of Electrochemistry - Reaction Feasibility (1), downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/7a8cb27862f6-5-3-principles-of-electrochemistry-reaction-feas.png)

![Electrochemical reactions showing oxidation of Cu²⁺ to Cu with E°=+0.34V and reduction of Cl₂ to 2Cl⁻ with E°=+1.36V, including half and overall equations.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/c084a207bc21-47629-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021025-3-p.png)

*A reaction is feasible when the standard cell potential Eꝋ is positive*

> **Exam Hint**
> Remember that the electrons only move through the wires in the external circuit and not through the electrolyte solution.

## Redox Equations

> **Spec point** — `24.2.7`

## Redox Equations

- The main ways to construct redox equations using the relevant half-equations:

  - Using changes in oxidation numbers to help balance chemical equations
  - Using the number of electrons for each half-cell
  
    - Both of these are discussed in the [Redox Reactions](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/chemistry/cie/25/revision-notes/6-electrochemistry/6-1-redox-processes-electron-transfer-and-changes-in-oxidation-number-oxidation-state/redox-reactions/) topic
  - Interpreting the information given to you and predicting any other chemicals involved in the reaction

> **Worked Example**
> Write the balanced chemical equation for hydrogen iodide reacting with sulfuric acid to form hydrogen sulfide, iodine and one other product
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> - There are 2 possible methods:
> 
>   1. Using ionic half-equations
>   2. Interpreting the information and predicting any other chemicals involved
> 
> **Using ionic half-equations method:**
> 
> - **Step 1:** Identify possible half-equations from the information
> 
>   - Iodide → iodine
>   - Sulfuric acid → hydrogen sulfide
> - **Step 2:** Construct the half equations
> 
>   - Iodide → iodine
>   
>     - I<sup>–</sup> → I<sub>2</sub>
>     - This requires 2 iodide ions and 2 electrons as products to balance the equation
>     - 2I<sup>–</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup>
>   - Sulfuric acid → hydrogen sulfide
>   
>     - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S
>     - The 4 oxygen atoms will form 4 water molecules as products
>     - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
>     - The 8 hydrogen atoms in the water molecules will require 8 protons as reactants
>     - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 8H<sup>+</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
>     - The 8 protons will require 8 electrons to balance the charge
>     - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 8e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> - **Step 3:** Combine the half-equations
> 
>   - Iodide → iodine
>   
>     - 2I<sup>–</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>–</sup>
>     - The iodide half-equation needs to be multiplied by 4 to have the same number of electrons as the sulfuric acid half-equation
>     - 8I<sup>–</sup> → 4I<sub>2</sub> + 8e<sup>–</sup>
>   - Sulfuric acid → hydrogen sulfide
>   
>     - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 8e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
>   - Combining the half-equations
>   
>     - 8I<sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 8e<sup>–</sup> → 4I<sub>2</sub> + 8e<sup>–</sup> H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
>   - Cancelling, where appropriate
>   
>     - The electrons cancel on both sides
>     - The 8I<sup>–</sup> and 8H<sup>+</sup> can be re-written as 8HI
>     - 8HI + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → 4I<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> **Interpreting and predicting method:**
> 
> - **Step 1:** Start with what you know:
> 
>   - HI + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S + I<sub>2</sub>
> - **Step 2:** Consider any elements that are not accounted for
> 
>   - The only element that is not currently considered is oxygen
> - **Step 3:** Make a common and appropriate suggestion for the missing product
> 
>   - Most of these questions are in solution so there is always H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>-</sup> available
>   - Missing product suggestion = 4H<sub>2</sub>O
>   - HI + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S + I<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> - **Step 4:** Balance the remaining chemicals
> 
>   - 8HI + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S + 4I<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

> **Exam Hint**
> - Similar approaches can be used to balance more complicated ionic half-equations
> - In these situations, you will have H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sup>+</sup>, OH<sup>-</sup> and electrons available

title: Nernst Equation
bodyMd:
# Nernst Equation

## The Nernst Equation

> **Spec point** — `24.2.9`

## The Nernst Equation

- Under non-standard conditions, the cell potential of the half-cells is shown by the symbol *E*<sub>*cell*</sub>
- The effect of changes in **temperature** and **ion concentration** on the *E*<sub>*cell*</sub> can be deduced using the **Nernst equation**

$E = E^{ } \Theta + \frac{ R T}{ z F} l n \frac{ \text{stretchy} [ oxidised species \text{stretchy} ]}{ \text{stretchy} [ reduced species \text{stretchy} ]}$

- ***E*** = electrode potential under nonstandard conditions

  - ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** **= standard electrode potential
  - ***R*** = gas constant (8.31 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>)
  - ***T*** = temperature (kelvin, K)
  - **z** = number of electrons transferred in the reaction
  - ***F***** **= Faraday constant (96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>)
  - **ln** = natural logarithm

- This equation can be simplified to

$E = E^{ } \Theta + \frac{ 0 . 059}{ z} log_{ } 10 \frac{ \text{stretchy} [ oxidised species \text{stretchy} ]}{ \text{stretchy} [ reduced species \text{stretchy} ]}$

- At standard temperature, *R, T* and *F* are constant

  - ln x = 2.303 log<sub>10</sub> x
- The Nernst equation only depends on **aqueous ions **and **not solids or gases**
- The concentrations of solids and gases are therefore set to 1.0 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the electrode potential of a Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup>** / Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup>** half-cell**
> 
> Calculate the electrode potential at 298K of a Fe<sup>3+</sup> / Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-cell.
> 
> Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> $\rightleftharpoons$ Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq)
> 
> - [Fe<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.034 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> - [Fe<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.64 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> - *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.77 V
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - From the question, the relevant values for the Fe<sup>3+ </sup>/ Fe<sup>2+</sup> half-cell are:
> 
>   - [Fe<sup>3+</sup>] = 0.034 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
>   - [Fe<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.64 mol dm<sup>-3 </sup>
>   - *E*<sup>Θ</sup> = + 0.77 V
> - The oxidised species is Fe<sup>3+</sup> as it has a higher oxidation number (+3)
> - The reduced species is Fe<sup>2+</sup> as it has a lower oxidation number (+2)
> - *z* is 1 as only one electron is transferred in this reaction
> - The Nernst equation for this half-reaction is, therefore:
> 
>   - $E = 0 . 77 + \frac{ 0 . 059}{ 1} log_{ } 10 \frac{ [ 0.034 ] }{ [ 0.64 ] }$
>   - ***E *****= (+0.77) + (-0.075)**
>   - ***E *****= +0.69 V**

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the electrode potential of a Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** / Cu half-cell**
> 
> Calculate the electrode potential at 298K of a Cu<sup>2+</sup> / Cu half-cell.
> 
> Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> $\rightleftharpoons$ Cu (s)
> 
> - [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.001 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> - *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +0.34 V
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - From the question, the relevant values for the Cu<sup>2+</sup> / Cu half-cell are:
> 
>   - [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] = 0.0010 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
>   - *E*<sup>Θ</sup> = + 0.34 V
> - The oxidised species is Cu<sup>2+</sup> as it has a higher oxidation number (+2)
> - The reduced species is Cu as it has a lower oxidation number (0)
> - Cu is solid which means that it is not included in the Nernst equation
> 
>   - Its concentration does not change and is, therefore, fixed at 1.0
> - *z* is 2 as 2 electrons are transferred in this reaction
> - The Nernst equation for this half-reaction is, therefore:
> 
>   - $E = E^{ } \Theta + \frac{ 0 . 059}{ z} log_{ } 10 \frac{ \text{stretchy} [ oxidised species \text{stretchy} ]}{ \text{stretchy} [ reduced species \text{stretchy} ]}$
>   - $E = 0 . 34 + \frac{ 0 . 059}{ 2} log_{ } 10 \frac{ [ 0.0010 ] }{ [ 1.0 ] }$
>   - ***E ***** = (+ 0.34) + (– 0.089)**
>   - ***E *****= + 0.25 V**

> **Exam Hint**
> - You need to know the Nernst equation, so make sure you learn it
> 
>   - CIE specifically ask students to learn use this version:
> 
> $E = E^{ } \Theta + \frac{ 0 . 059}{ z} log_{ } 10 \frac{ \text{stretchy} [ oxidised species \text{stretchy} ]}{ \text{stretchy} [ reduced species \text{stretchy} ]}$
> 
> - Make sure you always check what the temperature is
> - If the temperature is **not** 298 K (or 25 <sup>o</sup>C) the full Nernst equation should be used
> - You don’t need to know how to **simplify **the Nernst equation
> - You are only expected to use the equation when the temperature is 298 K (or 25 <sup>o</sup>C)

title: Non-Standard Conditions
bodyMd:
# Non-Standard Conditions

## Effect of Concentration on Electrode Potential

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_hvf4st7tCCknW7Dv`

## Effect of Concentration on Electrode Potential

- Changes in **temperature** and **concentration** of aqueous ions will affect the standard electrode potential (*E*<sup>ꝋ</sup>) of a half-cell
- Under these **non-standard conditions**, *E* is used as a symbol for the electrode potential instead of *E*<sup>ꝋ</sup>

### Increasing the concentration of the species on the left

- If the concentration of the species on the left is increased, the position of equilibrium will shift to the **right**
- This means that the species on the left gets **more** **easily** **reduced**
- The *E* value becomes **more positive **(or less negative)
- Let’s look at the half-cell below as an example

**Zn**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Zn (s)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**= -0.76 V**

- If the concentration of Zn<sup>2+</sup> (**species on the left**) is **increased**, the equilibrium position will shift to the **right**
- The species on the **left **(Zn<sup>2+</sup>) will get **more easily reduced**
- Therefore, the *E* value becomes **less negative** and will change too, for example, -0.50 V instead
- This principle can also be applied to a half-cell with a positive *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value such as:

**Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup>** (aq) + e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +0.77 V**

- If the concentration of Fe<sup>3+</sup> (**species on the left**) is **increased**, the equilibrium position will shift to the **right**
- The species on the **left **(Fe<sup>3+</sup>) will get more easily **reduced**
- Therefore, the *E* value becomes **more positive** and will change too, for example, +0.89 V instead

### Increasing the concentration of species on the right

- If the concentration of the species on the right is increased, the position of equilibrium will shift to the **left**
- This means that the species on the left get **less** **easily** **reduced**
- The *E* value becomes **less positive **(or more negative)
- Let’s look again at the half-cell below

**Zn**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Zn (s)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**= -0.76 V**

- If the concentration of Zn (**species on the right**) is **increased**, the equilibrium position will shift to the **left**
- The species on the **left **(Zn<sup>2+</sup>) will get less easily **reduced**
- Therefore, the *E* value becomes **more negative** and will change too, for example, -0.82 V instead
- This principle can, again, also be applied to a half-cell with a positive *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value:

**Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup>** (aq) + e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +0.77 V**

- If the concentration of Fe<sup>2+</sup> (**species on the right**) is **increased**, the equilibrium position will shift to the **left**
- The species on the **left **(Fe<sup>3+</sup>) will get less easily **reduced**
- Therefore, the *E* value becomes **less positive** and will change too, for example, +0.56 V instead

#### Effect of concentration on the electrode potential

![Diagram showing equilibrium shifts. Increasing reactants shifts equilibrium right, making E more positive. Increasing products shifts equilibrium left, making E less positive.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/bf2b084f394d-18540-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-4-e.png)

*Summarising the effects of changing the concentration of reactants and products*

title: Standard Cell Potential: Calculations, Electron Flow & Feasibility
bodyMd:
# Standard Cell Potential: Calculations, Electron Flow & Feasibility

## Standard Cell Potential Calculations

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_zJ3sxYXqq83ptdB6`

## Standard Cell Potential Calculations

- Once the ***E***<sup>ꝋ </sup>of a half-cell is known, the **potential difference** or **voltage** or** emf** of an **electrochemical cell **made up of any two half-cells can be calculated

  - These could be **any** half-cells and neither have to be a standard hydrogen electrode
- The **standard cell potential (***E*<sub>*cell*</sub><sup>ꝋ</sup>) can be calculated by **subtracting **the **less** **positive** *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>from the **more positive ***E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value

  - The half-cell with the more positive *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value will be the **positive** pole
  - By convention this is shown on the right-hand side in a conventional cell diagram, so is termed ** *****E***<sub>***right***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>
- The half-cell with the less positive *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value will be the **negative **pole

  - By convention this is shown on the left-hand side in a conventional cell diagram, so is termed ** *****E***<sub>***left***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>

***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = *****E***<sub>***right***</sub><sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**- *****E***<sub>***left***</sub><sup>**ꝋ   **</sup>

- Since oxidation is always on the left and reduction on the right, you can also use this version

***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = *****E***<sub>***reduction***</sub><sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**- *****E***<sub>***oxidation***</sub><sup>***ꝋ***</sup>

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the standard cell potential**
> 
> Calculate the standard cell potential for the electrochemical cell below and explain why the Cu<sup>2+ </sup>/ Cu half-cell is the positive pole. The half-equations are as follows:
> 
> **Cu**<sup>**2+ **</sup>**(aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Cu (s)      *****E***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**= +0.34 V**
> 
> **Zn**<sup>**2+ **</sup>**(aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Zn (s)      *****E***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**= −0.76 V**
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Calculate the standard cell potential. The copper is more positive so must be the right hand side.
> 
> *E*<sub>*cell*</sub><sup>ꝋ</sup> = *E*<sub>*right*</sub><sup>ꝋ </sup>- *E*<sub>*left*</sub><sup>ꝋ   </sup>
> 
> *E*<sub>*cell*</sub><sup>ꝋ</sup> = (+0.34) - (-0.76) = +1.10 V
> 
> - **Step 2: **Determine the positive and negative poles
> 
> ![Diagram showing oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode, with the overall ionic equation of zinc and copper ions forming zinc ions and copper.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/1e3e60775a80-56616-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021069-1-9.png)
> 
> - The Cu<sup>2+ </sup>/ Cu  half-cell is the **positive** pole as its *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>is more positive than the *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value of the Zn<sup>2+ </sup>/ Zn half-cell

> **Exam Hint**
> - Students often confuse the redox process that take place in voltaic cells and electrolytic cells.
> - An easy way to remember is the phrase RED CATS: REDuction takes place at the CAThode.  OR AN OX. OXidation takes place at the ANode

## Electrochemical Series

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_yF7qm8h6B4HYtHhS`

## Electrochemical Series

- The *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>values of a species indicate how **easily **they can get **oxidised **or **reduced**
- In other words, they indicate the relative **reactivity **of elements, compounds and ions as **oxidising agents** or **reducing agents**
- The **electrochemical series **is a list of various **redox equilibria** in order of decreasing *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>values
- **More positive **(less negative) *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>values indicate that:

  - The species is easily **reduced**
  - The species is a better **oxidising agent**
- **Less positive **(more negative) *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>values indicate that:

  - The species is easily **oxidised**
  - The species is a better **reducing agent**

#### An example electrochemical series

![Table of redox reactions showing oxidising and reducing agents with electrode potentials. Arrows indicate increasing oxidising and reducing power.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/946a17ce23ed-58468-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021025-4-e.png)

*In this example electrochemical series the equilibria are arranged in order of decreasing Eꝋ values. These values can then be used to identify the strongest and weakest reducing / oxidising agents.*

title: Standard Electrode & Cell Potentials
bodyMd:
# Standard Electrode & Cell Potentials

## Standard Electrode & Standard Cell Potentials

> **Spec point** — `24.2.1`

## Standard Electrode & Standard Cell Potentials

### Electrode potential

- The **electrode (reduction) potential **(***E***) is a value which shows how easily a substance is **reduced**
- These are demonstrated using reversible half equations

  - This is because there is a redox equilibrium between two related species that are in different oxidation states
  - For example, if you dipped a zinc metal rod into a solution which contained zinc ions, there would be zinc atoms losing electrons to form zinc ions and at the same time, zinc ions gaining electrons to become zinc atoms
  - This would cause a redox equilibrium

#### Half equations

- When writing half equations for this topic, the electrons will always be written on the left-hand side (demonstrating reduction)
- The position of equilibrium is different for different species, which is why different species will have electrode (reduction) potentials
- The more **positive** (or less negative) an electrode potential, the **more likely** it is for that species to undergo **reduction**

  - The equilibrium position lies more to the **right**
- For example, the positive electrode potential of bromine below, suggests that it is likely to get reduced and form bromide (Br<sup>-</sup>) ions

**Br**<sub>**2**</sub>** (l) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ 2Br**<sup>**- **</sup>**(aq)        voltage = +1.09 V**

- The more **negative** (or less positive) the electrode potential, the less likely it is that reduction of that species will occur

  - The equilibrium position lies more to the **left**
- For example, the negative electrode potential of sodium suggests that it is unlikely that the sodium (Na<sup>+</sup>) ions will be reduced to sodium (Na) atoms

**Na**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Na (s)        voltage = -2.71 V**

### Standard electrode potential

- The position of equilibrium and therefore the electrode potential depends on factors such as:

  - Temperature
  - Pressure of gases
  - Concentration of reagents
- So, to be able to compare the electrode potentials of different species, they all have to be measured against a common reference or standard

#### Standard conditions

- **Standard** **conditions** also have to be used when comparing electrode potentials
- These standard conditions are:

  - An ion concentration of 1.00 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
  - A temperature of 298 K
  - A pressure of 1 atm

- The electrode potentials are measured relative to something called a **standard hydrogen electrode**
- The standard hydrogen electrode is given a value of 0.00 V, and all other electrode potentials are compared to this standard
- This means that the electrode potentials are always referred to as a **standard electrode potential** **(*****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>**)**
- The **standard electrode potential** **(*****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>**) **is the voltage produced when a **standard half-cell** is connected to a **standard hydrogen cell** under standard conditions
- For example, the standard electrode potential of bromine suggests that relative to the hydrogen half-cell it is more likely to get reduced, as it has a **more positive** *E*<sup>ꝋ</sup> value

**Br**<sub>**2**</sub>** (l) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ 2Br**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +1.09 V**

**2H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = 0.00 V**

- The standard electrode potential of sodium, on the other hand, suggests that relative to the hydrogen half-cell it is less likely to get reduced as it has a **more negative** *E*<sup>ꝋ</sup> value

**Na**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Na (s)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = -2.71 V**

**2H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = 0.00 V**

### Standard cell potential

- Once the ***E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup> of a half-cell is known, the **voltage **of an **electrochemical cell** made up of two half-cells can be calculated

  - These could be **any **half-cells and neither have to be a standard hydrogen electrode

- This is also known as the **standard cell potential** (***E***<sub>**cell**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>)
- The standard cell potential can be determined by two methods:

  1. Using the equation ***E***<sub>**cell**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** **= ***E***<sub>**reduction**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>*** – E***<sub>**oxidation**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>
  
    - Use of this equation does require knowledge of which reaction is reduction and which is oxidation
    - The reduction reaction has the higher / more positive *E*<sup>*ꝋ*</sup>* *value
  2. ***E***<sub>**cell**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** **is the difference in *E*<sup>ꝋ</sup> between two half-cells
- For example, an electrochemical cell consisting of bromine and sodium half-cells has an ***E***<sub>**cell**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** **of:

  - ***E***<sub>**cell**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** **= (+1.09) - (-2.71)
  - ***E***<sub>**cell**</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** **= +3.80 V

## Standard Hydrogen Electrode

> **Spec point** — `24.2.2`

## Standard Hydrogen Electrode

- When a metal rod is placed in an aqueous solution, a **redox equilibrium **is established between the metal ions and atoms

  - For example, the copper atoms get **oxidised** and enter the solution as copper ions

**Cu (s) → Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**-**</sup>

#### Oxidation of copper ions

![Diagram of copper electrodes in solutions showing copper atoms losing electrons to become copper 2+ ions, with arrows indicating the process.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/be92bac3a1af-5129-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads20250638284-.png)

*During oxidation, copper atoms lose 2 electrons to form copper ions*

- The copper ions gain electrons from the metal rod and deposit as metal atoms on the rod

**Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**→ Cu (s)**

#### Reduction of copper ions

![Diagram of copper electrodes in solutions showing copper atoms losing electrons to form copper 2+ ions, with ions moving between solutions.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/a4597be078fc-60131-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads20250638284.png)

*During reduction, copper ions gain 2 electrons to form copper atoms*

- When equilibrium is established, the **rate** of oxidation and reduction of copper is **equal**

- The position of the redox equilibrium is different for different metals

  - Copper is more easily **reduced**, thus the equilibrium lies further over to the **right**

**Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Cu (s)**

- Vanadium is more easily **oxidised**, thus the equilibrium lies further over to the **left**

**V**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ V(s)**

- The metal atoms and ions in solution cause an **electric potential **(**voltage**)
- This potential cannot be measured **directly** however the potential between the metal/metal ion system and **another** system **can** be measured
- This value is called the **electrode potential** (***E***) and is measured in **volts**

  - The electrode potential is the **voltage** measured for a half-cell compared to another half-cell
  - Often, the half-cell used for comparison is the **standard** **hydrogen** **electrode**

### Standard hydrogen electrode

- The **standard hydrogen electrode **is a half-cell used as a **reference electrode** and consists of:

  - Hydrogen gas in equilibrium with H<sup>+</sup> ions of concentration 1.00 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (at 1 atm)

**2H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**-**</sup>** ⇌ H**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g)**

- An **inert** **platinum **electrode that is in contact with the hydrogen gas and H<sup>+</sup> ions
- When the standard hydrogen electrode is connected to another half-cell, the **standard electrode potential **of that half-cell can be read off a voltmeter

#### The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)

![Diagram of a hydrogen electrode in a solution, featuring a platinum wire and electrode, with hydrogen gas at 1 atm and labelled elements.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/eadbb6ab92fe-15197-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021025-3-p.png)

*The standard electrode potential of a half-cell can be determined by connecting it to a standard hydrogen electrode*

title: Standard Electrode Potentials: Free Energy Change
bodyMd:
# Standard Electrode Potentials: Free Energy Change

## Free Energy Change Calculations Using Standard Electrode Potentials

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_9h2zdD3sCnvBMsK8`

## Calculating Free Energy Change Using Standard Electrode Potentials

- The **standard free energy change **can be calculated using the standard cell potential of an electrochemical cell

**Δ*****G***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = - n x *****E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** x *****F***

- **Δ*****G***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup> = standard Gibbs free energy

  - **n** = number of electrons transferred in the reaction
  - ***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup> = standard cell potential (V)
  - ***F*** = Faraday constant (96 500 C mol<sup>-1</sup>)

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the standard Gibbs free energy change**
> 
> Calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change for the following electrochemical cell:
> 
> 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s) ⇌ 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq)
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Determine the two half-equations and their *E*<sup>ꝋ</sup> using the Data booklet:
> 
> **Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup>** (aq) + e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)        *****E***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = +0.77 V**
> 
> **Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2e**<sup>**- **</sup>**⇌ Cu (s)       *****E***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>**= +0.34 V **
> 
> - **Step 2: **Calculate the *E*<sub>*cell*</sub><sup>ꝋ</sup>
> 
>   - ***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = *****E***<sub>***red***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** - *****E***<sub>***ox***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>
>   - ***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** ** = (+0.77) - (+0.34)
>   - ***E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** ** = +0.43 V
> 
> - **Step 3: **Determine the number of electrons transferred in the reaction
> 
>   - The Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu has a smaller *E*<sup>ꝋ </sup>value which means that it gets **oxidised**
>   - It **transfers **two electrons to  **two **Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions
>   - Each Fe<sup>3+</sup> ion accepts one electron so the total number of electrons transferred is **two**
> 
> - **Step 4: **Substitute the values in for the standard Gibbs free energy equation
> 
>   - **Δ*****G***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** = - n x *****E***<sub>***cell***</sub><sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** x *****F***
>   - **Δ*****G***<sup>**ꝋ**</sup>** ** = -2 x (+0.43) x 96 500
>   - **Δ*****G***<sup>**ꝋ **</sup>= -82 990 J mol<sup>-1</sup> = -83 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
