# Buffer Calculations

## Buffer Solution pH Calculations

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_mJRT89K2QYQn2gqs`

## Buffer Solution pH Calculations

- The pH of a **buffer** **solution** can be calculated using:

  - The *K*<sub>*a*</sub>* *of the **weak acid**
  - The **equilibrium concentration **of the **weak acid **and its **conjugate base** (salt)
- To determine the pH, the concentration of **hydrogen** **ions **is needed which can be found using the equilibrium expression:

***K***<sub>**a**</sub>** =** $\frac{[ \text{salt} ] [ H^{+} ]}{[ \text{acid} ]}$

- This can be rearranged to determine the concentration of hydrogen ions:

**[H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] = **$K_{ } a \times \frac{ \text{stretchy} [ \text{acid} \text{stretchy} ]}{ \text{stretchy} [ \text{salt} \text{stretchy} ]}$

- To simplify the calculations, **logarithms **are used such that the expression becomes:

**–log**<sub>**10**</sub>** [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] = **$- log_{ } 10 K_{ } a \times - log_{ } 10 \frac{ \text{stretchy} [ \text{acid} \text{stretchy} ]}{ \text{stretchy} [ \text{salt} \text{stretchy} ]}$

- Since -log<sub>10</sub> [H<sup>+</sup>] = pH and -log<sub>10</sub> [*K*<sub>a</sub>] = p*K*<sub>a</sub>, the expression can also be rewritten as:

$pH = p K_{ } a a + log_{ } 10 \frac{ \text{stretchy} [ \text{salt} \text{stretchy} ]}{ \text{stretchy} [ \text{acid} \text{stretchy} ]}$

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the pH of a buffer solution**
> 
> Calculate the pH of a buffer solution containing 0.305 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> ethanoic acid and 0.520 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> sodium ethanoate.
> 
> The *K*<sub>a</sub> of ethanoic acid = 1.43 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - Ethanoic acid is a weak acid that ionises as follows:
> 
> **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COOH (aq) ⇌ H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COO**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Write down the equilibrium expression to find *K*<sub>a</sub>:
> 
> *K*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{[ CH_{3} COO^{-} ] [ \mathrm{H}^{+} ]}{[ CH_{3} \text{COOH} ]}$
> 
> - **Step 2: **Rearrange the equation to find [H<sup>+</sup>]:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>a</sub> x $\frac{[ CH_{3} \text{COOH} ]}{[ CH_{3} COO^{-} ]}$
> 
> - **Step 3: **Substitute the values into the expression:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.43 x 10<sup>-5</sup> x $\frac{[ 0.305 ]}{[ 0.520 ]}$
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 8.39 x 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> - **Step 4: **Calculate the pH:
> 
> pH = –log<sub>10</sub> [H<sup>+</sup>]
> 
> pH = –log 8.39 x 10<sup>-6</sup>
> 
> pH = 5.08

title: Buffers
bodyMd:
# Buffers

## Buffers

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_YXgprkBMDtsH6nb3`

## Buffers

- A **buffer solution **is a solution in which the pH does not change a lot when small amounts of acids or alkalis are added

  - A buffer solution is used to keep the pH almost constant
  - A buffer can consist of a **weak acid - conjugate base **or a **weak base - conjugate acid**

### Ethanoic acid & sodium ethanoate as a buffer

- A common buffer solution is an **aqueous mixture of ethanoic acid **and **sodium ethanoate**
- Ethanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, is a **weak acid **and partially ionises in solution to form a relatively **low **concentration of **ethanoate ions**, CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup>

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COOH (aq) **$\rightleftharpoons$** H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COO**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq)**

- Sodium ethanoate, CH<sub>3</sub>COONa, is a **salt** which fully ionises in solution to form a relatively **high **concentration of **ethanoate ions**, CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup>

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COONa (a) + aq → Na**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COO**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq)**

- There are **reserve supplies **of the acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) and its conjugate base (CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>)

  - The buffer solution contains relatively high concentrations of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (due to the ionisation of **ethanoic** **acid**) and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (due to the ionisation of **sodium** **ethanoate**)
- In the **buffer solution**, the ethanoic acid is **in equilibrium **with hydrogen and ethanoate ions

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COOH (aq) **$\rightleftharpoons$**H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq)  + CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COO**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq)**

#### When H<sup>+</sup> ions are added:

- The equilibrium position shifts to the **left** as H<sup>+ </sup>ions react with CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> ions to form more CH<sub>3</sub>COOH until equilibrium is **re-established**
- As there is a large reserve supply of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup>, the concentration of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> in solution doesn’t change much as it reacts with the added H<sup>+ </sup>ions
- As there is a large reserve supply of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, the concentration of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH in solution doesn’t change much as CH<sub>3</sub>COOH is formed from the reaction of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> with H<sup>+</sup>
- As a result, the pH remains reasonably constant

#### When OH<sup>-</sup> ions are added:

- The OH<sup>-</sup> reacts with H<sup>+</sup> to form water

**OH**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq) + H**<sup>**+  **</sup>**(aq) → H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)**

- The H<sup>+</sup> concentration **decreases**
- The equilibrium position shifts to the right and more CH<sub>3</sub>COOH molecules ionise to form more H<sup>+</sup> and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> until equilibrium is re-established

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COOH (aq) → H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COO**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**

- As there is a large reserve supply of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH the concentration of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH in solution doesn’t change much when CH<sub>3</sub>COOH dissociates to form more H<sup>+ </sup>ions
- As there is a large reserve supply of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> the concentration of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> in solution doesn’t change much
- As a result, the pH remains reasonably constant

### Uses of buffer solutions in controlling the pH of blood

- In humans, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ions act as a buffer to keep the blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45
- Body cells produce CO<sub>2</sub> during **aerobic respiration**
- This CO<sub>2</sub> will combine with water in the blood to form a solution containing H<sup>+</sup> ions

**CO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) ⇌ H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) + HCO**<sub>**3**</sub><sup>**- **</sup>**(aq)**

- This equilibrium between CO<sub>2</sub> and HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>- </sup>is extremely important
- If the concentration of H<sup>+ </sup>ions is not regulated, the blood pH would drop and cause ‘**acidosis**’

  - **Acidosis **refers to a condition in which there is too much acid in the body fluids such as blood
  - This could cause body malfunctioning and eventually lead to coma
- **If there is an increase in H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**ions**
- The equilibrium position shifts to the **left **until equilibrium is restored

**CO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) → H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) + HCO**<sub>**3**</sub><sup>**- **</sup>**(aq)**

- This reduces the concentration of H<sup>+</sup> and keeps the pH of the blood **constant**
- **If there is a decrease in H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**ions**

  - The equilibrium position shifts to the **right **until equilibrium is restored

**CO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) → H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) + HCO**<sub>**3**</sub><sup>**- **</sup>**(aq)**

- This increases the concentration of H<sup>+</sup> and keeps the pH of the blood **constant**

> **Exam Hint**
> - Remember that buffer solutions cannot cope with **excessive addition **of acids or alkalis as their pH will change significantly
> - The pH will only remain relatively constant if **small amounts **of acids or alkalis are added.

title: Conjugate Acids & Bases
bodyMd:
# Conjugate Acids & Bases

## Conjugate Acids & Bases

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_z6tmpdvg4TZhmwV7`

## Conjugate Acids & Bases

- A **Brønsted-Lowry acid **is a species that can donate a proton
- A **Brønsted-Lowry base **is a species that can accept a proton
- In an equilibrium reaction, the products are formed at the same rate as the reactants are used

CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)         ⇌    CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>- </sup>(aq)          +         H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> (aq)

acid                 base                    conjugate base             conjugate acid

- The reactant CH<sub>3</sub>COOH is linked to the product CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>- </sup>by the transfer of a **proton **from the acid to the base

  - Similarly, the H<sub>2</sub>O molecule is linked to H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ion by the transfer of a proton
- These pairs are therefore called **conjugate acid-base pairs**

  - A **conjugate acid-base pair** is two species that are different from each other by a H<sup>+</sup> ion
  
    - **Conjugate **here means related
    - In other words, the acid and base are related to each other by one proton difference

> **Worked Example**
> **Identifying conjugate acid-base pairs**
> 
> Identify the conjugate acid-base pairs in the following equilibrium reaction:
> 
> **NH**<sub>**3**</sub>** (g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) **$\rightleftharpoons$** NH**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + OH**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq)**
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> - In the forward reaction:
> 
>   - NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> is the conjugate acid of the base NH<sub>3</sub>
>   - OH<sup>-</sup> is the conjugate base of the acid H<sub>2</sub>O
> - In the reverse reaction
> 
>   - NH<sub>3</sub> is the conjugate base of the acid NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>
>   - H<sub>2</sub>O is the conjugate acid of the base OH<sup>–</sup>
> 
> ![Equilibria - Conjugate Acid-Base Pair, downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/cc7d0f16b271-5-5-equilibria-conjugate-acid-base-pair.png)

> **Worked Example**
> In the equilibrium reaction shown below, which species are a conjugate acid-base pair?
> 
> **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**COOH (aq)  +  H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) ⇌ CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**COO**<sup>**- **</sup>**(aq)  +  H**<sub>**3**</sub>**O**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) **
> 
> **   A**.    CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH and H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> **   B**.    H<sub>2</sub>O and H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> 
> **   C**.    H<sub>2</sub>O and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>-</sup>
> 
> **   D**.   CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>- </sup>and H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> 
> **Answer:**
> 
> - The correct option in **B**
> 
>   - A conjugate acid-base pair differ only by an H<sup>+</sup> ion

title: pH & [H+] Calculations
bodyMd:
# pH & [H+] Calculations

## [H+] & pH Calculations

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_rcYTTx2Xn8VynVS7`

## [H+] & pH Calculations

- If the concentration of H<sup>+</sup> of an acid or alkali is known, the **pH** can be calculated using the equation:

**pH = -log [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**]**

- Similarly, the **concentration** **of** **H**<sup>**+**</sup>** **of a solution can be calculated if the pH is known by rearranging the above equation to:

**[H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] = 10**<sup>**-pH**</sup>

### Strong acids

- **Strong acids** are completely **ionised **in solution

**HA (aq) → H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + A**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**

- Therefore, the concentration of hydrogen ions ([H<sup>+</sup>]) is **equal **to the concentration of acid ([HA])
- The number of hydrogen ions ([H<sup>+</sup>]) formed from the ionisation of water is **very small **relative to the [H<sup>+</sup>] due to the ionisation of the strong acid and can therefore be **neglected**
- The **total **[H<sup>+</sup>] is therefore the same as the [HA]

> **Worked Example**
> **pH calculations of a strong acid**
> 
> For a solution of hydrochloric acid, calculate the following:
> 
> 1. The pH when the hydrogen ion concentration is 1.6 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 2. The hydrogen ion concentration when the pH is 3.1.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - Hydrochloric acid is a strong monobasic acid
> 
> **HCl (aq) → H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + Cl**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**
> 
> **Answer 1**
> 
> - The pH of the solution is:
> 
> pH = -log [H<sup>+</sup>]
> 
> pH = -log 1.6 x 10<sup>-4</sup>
> 
> pH = 3.80
> 
> **Answer 2**
> 
> - The hydrogen concentration can be calculated by rearranging the equation for pH:
> 
> pH = -log [H<sup>+</sup>]
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-pH</sup>
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-3.1</sup>
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 7.9 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

### Strong alkalis

- **Strong alkalis **are completely **ionised **in solution

**BOH (aq) → B**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + OH**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**

- Therefore, the concentration of hydroxide ions ([OH<sup>-</sup>]) is **equal **to the concentration of base ([BOH])

  - Even strong alkalis have small amounts of H<sup>+</sup> in solution which is due to the ionisation of water
- The concentration of OH<sup>-</sup> in solution can be used to calculate the pH using the **ionic product of water**

***K***<sub>**w**</sub>** = [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] [OH**<sup>**-**</sup>**]**

**[H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] = **$\frac{ K_{ } w}{ \text{stretchy} [ OH^{ - } \text{stretchy} ]}$

- Since *K*<sub>w</sub> is 1.00 x 10<sup>-14</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

**[H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] = **$\frac{1 . 00 \times 10^{- 14} }{[ OH^{-} ]}$

- Once the [H<sup>+</sup>] has been determined, the pH of the strong alkali can be found using pH = -log[H<sup>+</sup>]
- Similarly, the ionic product of water can be used to find the concentration of OH<sup>-</sup> ions in solution if [H<sup>+</sup>] is known

**[OH**<sub>**–**</sub>**] = **$\frac{1 . 00 \times 10^{- 14} }{[ H^{+} ]}$

> **Worked Example**
> **pH calculations of a strong alkali**
> 
> For a solution of sodium hydroxide, calculate the following:
> 
> 1. The pH when the hydrogen ion concentration is 3.5 x 10<sup>-11</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 2. The hydroxide ion concentration when the pH is 12.3.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - Sodium hydroxide is a strong base which ionises as follows:
> 
> **NaOH (aq) → Na**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + OH**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq) **
> 
> **Answer 1**
> 
> - The pH of the solution is:
> 
> pH = -log [H<sup>+</sup>]
> 
> pH = -log 3.5 x 10<sup>-11</sup>
> 
> pH = 10.5
> 
> **Answer 2**
> 
> - **Step 1:** Calculate the hydrogen concentration by rearranging the equation for pH:
> 
> pH = -log [H<sup>+</sup>]
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-pH</sup>
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>-12.3</sup>
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 5.01 x 10<sup>-13</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> - **Step 2: **Rearrange the **ionic product of water**  to find the concentration of hydroxide ions:
> 
> *K*<sub>w</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>] [OH<sup>-</sup>]
> 
> [OH<sup>–</sup>] = $\frac{K_{w} }{[ \mathrm{H}^{+} ]}$
> 
> - **Step 3: **Substitute the values into the expression to find the concentration of hydroxide ions:
> 
>   - Since *K*<sub>*w*</sub> is 1.00 x 10<sup>-14</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>
> - [OH<sup>–</sup>] = $\frac{1.00\times10^{-14}}{5.01\times10^{-13}}$
> - [OH<sup>–</sup>] = 0.0199<sup> </sup>mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

### Weak acids

- The pH of **weak acids** can be calculated when the following is known:

  - The **concentration** of the acid
  - The ***K***<sub>***a***</sub> value of the acid

> **Worked Example**
> **pH calculations of weak acids**
> 
> Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> ethanoic acid at 298K with a *K*<sub>a</sub> value of 1.74 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - Ethanoic acid is a weak acid which ionises as follows:
> 
> **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COOH (aq) ⇌ H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COO**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Write down the equilibrium expression to find *K*<sub>a</sub>:
> 
> *K*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{[ \mathrm{H} + ] [ CH_{3} COO^{-} ]}{[ CH_{3} \text{COOH} ]}$
> 
> - **Step 2: **Simplify the expression:
> 
>   - The ratio of H<sup>+</sup> to CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> ions is 1:1
>   - Therefore the concentration of H<sup>+</sup> and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> ions are the same
>   - So, the expression can be simplified to:
> 
> *K*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{[ \mathrm{H} + ]^{2}}{[ CH_{3} \text{COOH} ]}$
> 
> - **Step 3: **Rearrange the expression to find [H<sup>+</sup>]:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = $\sqrt{K_{a} \times [ CH_{3} \text{COOH} ]}$
> 
> - **Step 4: **Substitute the values into the expression to find [H<sup>+</sup>]:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = $\sqrt{( 1.74 \times 10^{- 5} ) \times 0.100}$
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.32 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> - **Step 5: **Find the pH:
> 
> pH = -log<sub>10</sub> [H<sup>+</sup>]
> 
> pH = -log<sub>10</sub> 1.32 x 10<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> pH = 2.88

title: pH, Ka, pKa & Kw Calculations
bodyMd:
# pH, Ka, pKa & Kw Calculations

## Calculating pH, Ka, pKA & Kw

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_m7HVCDD4RZSvGKzJ`

## Calculating pH, Ka, pKA & Kw

### pH

- The **pH** indicates the **acidity** or **basicity** of an acid or alkali
- The pH scale goes from 0.0 to 14.0

  - Acids have a pH below 7.0
  - Pure water is **neutral **with a pH of 7.0
  - Bases and alkalis have a pH above 7.0
- pH can be calculated using:

**pH = -log**<sub>**10**</sub>** [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**]**

- where [H<sup>+</sup>] = concentration of H<sup>+</sup> ions (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)
- The pH can also be used to calculate the concentration of H<sup>+</sup> ions in solution by rearranging the equation to:

**[H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] = 10**<sup>**-pH**</sup>

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the pH of acids**
> 
> Calculate the pH of ethanoic acid, at 298K, when the hydrogen ion concentration is 1.32 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> pH = -log [H<sup>+</sup>]
> 
> pH = -log 1.32 x 10<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> pH = 2.9

### K<sub>a</sub> & pK<sub>a</sub>

- The *K*<sub>a</sub> is the **acidic dissociation constant**

  - It is the **equilibrium constant **for the dissociation of a **weak** **acid** at 298 K
- For the **partial** **ionisation** of a weak acid HA, the equilibrium expression to find *K*<sub>a</sub> is:

**HA (aq) ⇌ H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + A**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**

***K***<sub>**a**</sub>*** = ***$\frac{[ H + ] [ A^{-} ]}{[ \text{HA} ]}$

- When writing the equilibrium expression for weak acids, the following assumptions are made:

  - The concentration of hydrogen ions due to the ionisation of water is negligible
  - The dissociation of the weak acid is so small that the concentration of HA can be approximated by its initial value
  
    - This is calculated from the number of moles divided by the volume of solvent
- The value of *K*<sub>a</sub> indicates the extent of dissociation

  - A high value of *K*<sub>a</sub> means that:
  
    - The equilibrium position lies to the right
    - The acid is **almost** **completely** **ionised**
    - The acid is **strongly acidic**
  - A low value of *K*<sub>a</sub> means that:
  
    - The equilibrium position lies to the left
    - The acid is **only slightly ionised** (there are mainly HA and only a few H<sup>+</sup> and A<sup>-</sup> ions)
    - The acid is **weakly acidic**
- Since *K*<sub>a</sub> values of many weak acids are **very low**, p*K*<sub>a</sub>* *values are used instead to compare the strengths of weak acids with each other

**p*****K***<sub>**a**</sub>** = -log**<sub>**10**</sub>** *****K***<sub>**a**</sub>

- The **less** **positive** the p*K*<sub>a</sub> value the **more** **acidic** the acid is

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the *****K***<sub>***a***</sub>*** *****& p*****K***<sub>***a***</sub>** of weak acids**
> 
> Calculate the *K*<sub>a</sub>* *and p*K*<sub>a</sub> values of 0.100 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> ethanoic acid at 298K which forms 1.32 x 10<sup>-3</sup> of H<sup>+</sup> ions in solution.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Write down the equation for the partial dissociation of ethanoic acid:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (aq) ⇌ H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (aq)
> 
> - **Step 2: **Write down the equilibrium expression to find *K*<sub>a</sub>:
> 
> *K*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{[ \mathrm{H}^{+} ] [ CH_{3} COO^{-} ]}{[ CH_{3} \text{COOH} ]}$
> 
> - **Step 3: **Simplify the expression:
> 
> The ratio of H<sup>+</sup> to CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> is 1:1
> 
> The concentration of H<sup>+</sup> and CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> is, therefore, the same
> 
> The equilibrium expression can be simplified to:
> 
> *K*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{[ \mathrm{H}^{+} ]^{2}}{[ CH_{3} \text{COOH} ]}$
> 
> - **Step 4: **Substitute the values into the expression to find *K*<sub>a</sub>:
> 
> *K*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{[ 1.32 \times 10^{- 3} ]^{2}}{[ 0.100 ]}$
> 
> *K*<sub>a</sub> = 1.74 x 10<sup>-5</sup>
> 
> - **Step 5: **Determine the units of *K*<sub>a</sub>:
> 
> *K*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{[ \text{mol} dm^{- 3} ]^{2}}{[ \text{mol} dm^{- 3} ]}$= mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> Therefore, *K*<sub>a</sub> is 1.74 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> - **Step 6: **Find p*K*<sub>a</sub>:
> 
> p*K*<sub>a</sub> = - log<sub>10 </sub>*K*<sub>a</sub>
> 
> p*K*<sub>a</sub><sub>* *</sub>*=* - log<sub>10</sub> (1.74 x 10<sup>-5</sup>)
> 
> p*K*<sub>a</sub> = 4.76

### K<sub>w</sub>

- The *K*<sub>w</sub> is the **ionic product of water**

  - It is the **equilibrium constant **for the dissociation of **water** at 298 K
  - Its value is 1.00 x 10<sup>-14</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>
- For the **ionisation** of water, the equilibrium expression to find *K*<sub>w</sub> is:

**H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) ⇌ H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + OH**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**

***K***<sub>**w**</sub>** = **$\frac{[ H^{+} ] [ OH^{-} ]}{[ H_{2} O ]}$

- As the **extent of ionisation **is very low, only small amounts of H<sup>+</sup> and  OH<sup>- </sup>ions are formed
- The concentration of H<sub>2</sub>O can therefore be regarded as constant and removed from the *K*<sub>*w*</sub> expression
- The equilibrium expression therefore becomes:

***K***<sub>**w**</sub>** = [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] [OH**<sup>**-**</sup>**]**

- As the [H<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>+</sup>] in pure water, the equilibrium expression can be further simplified to:

***K***<sub>**w**</sub>** = [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**]**<sup>**2**</sup>

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the concentration of H**<sup>**+**</sup>** of pure water**
> 
> Calculate the concentration of H<sup>+</sup> in pure water, using the ionic product of water
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Write down the equation for the partial dissociation of water:
> 
>   - In pure water, the following equilibrium exists:
> 
> **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) ⇌ H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + OH**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**
> 
> - **Step 2: **Write down the equilibrium expression to find *K*<sub>w</sub>:
> 
> ***K***<sub>**w**</sub>** = **$\frac{[ H^{+} ] [ OH^{-} ]}{[ H_{2} O ]}$
> 
> - **Step 3: **Simplify the expression:
> 
>   - Since the concentration of H<sub>2</sub>O is constant, this expression can be simplified to:
> 
> ***K***<sub>**w**</sub>** = [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] [OH**<sup>**-**</sup>**]**
> 
> - **Step 4: **Further simplify the expression:
> 
>   - The ratio of H<sup>+</sup> to OH<sup>-</sup> is 1:1
>   - The concentration of H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>-</sup> is, therefore, the same and the equilibrium expression can be further simplified to:
> 
> ***K***<sub>**w**</sub>** = [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**]**<sup>**2**</sup>
> 
> - **Step 5: **Rearrange the equation to find [H<sup>+</sup>]:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = $\sqrt{K_{w}}$
> 
> - **Step 6: **Substitute the values into the expression to find *K*<sub>w</sub>:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = $\sqrt{1.00\times10^{-14}}$
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.00 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **Exam Hint**
> - The greater the *K*<sub>*a*</sub>* *value, the **more strongly acidic **the acid is
> - The greater the p*K*<sub>*a*</sub> value, the **less strongly acidic **the acid is.
> - Also, you should be able to rearrange the following expressions:
> 
> **pH = -log**<sub>**10**</sub>** [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**]   ⇔   [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] = 10**<sup>**-pH**</sup>
> 
> ***K***<sub>**a**</sub>** = **$\frac{[ H^{+} ] [ A^{-} ]}{[ \text{HA} ]}$**   ⇔    [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**] = **`equation`
> 
> **p*****K***<sub>**a**</sub>** = - log**<sub>**10 **</sub>***K***<sub>**a**</sub>**    ⇔   *****K***<sub>**a**</sub>** = 10**<sup>**-p**</sup><sup>***K***</sup><sup>**a**</sup>

# Solubility Product Calculations

## Solubility Product Calculations

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_NjwGX5WsGm4tfWS7`

## Solubility Product Calculations

- Calculations involving the **solubility product **(*K*<sub>*sp*</sub>) may include::

  - Calculating the solubility product of a compound from its **solubility**
  - Calculating the solubility of a compound from the **solubility** **product**

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the solubility product of a compound from its solubility**
> 
> Calculate the solubility product of a saturated solution of lead(II) bromide, PbBr<sub>2</sub>, with a solubility of 1.39 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Write down the equilibrium equation:
> 
> **PbBr**<sub>**2**</sub>** (s) ⇌ Pb**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2Br**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**
> 
> - **Step 2: **Write down the equilibrium expression:
> 
> ***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** = [Pb**<sup>**2+**</sup>**(aq)] [Br**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)]**<sup>**2**</sup>
> 
> - **Step 3: **Calculate the ion concentrations in the solution:
> 
>   - **[PbBr**<sub>**2**</sub>**(s)] = 1.39 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>
>   - The ratio of PbBr<sub>2</sub> to Pb<sup>2+</sup> is 1:1
> 
> **[Pb**<sup>**2+**</sup>**(aq)] = [PbBr**<sub>**2**</sub>**(s)] = 1.39 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>
> 
> - The ratio of PbBr<sub>2</sub> to Br<sup>-</sup> is 1:2
> 
> **[Br**<sup>**-**</sup>**(aq)] = 2 x [PbBr**<sub>**2**</sub>**(s)] = 2 x 1.39 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3 **</sup>**= 2.78 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>
> 
> - **Step 4: **Substitute the values into the expression to find the solubility product:
> 
> ***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** = (1.39 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>**) x (2.78 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>**)**<sup>**2**</sup>
> 
> ***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>*** *****= 1.07 x 10**<sup>**-8**</sup>
> 
> - **Step 6:  **Determine the correct units of *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>:
> 
> ***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** = (mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>**) x (mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>**)**<sup>**2**</sup>
> 
> ***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** = mol**<sup>**3**</sup>** dm**<sup>**-9**</sup>
> 
> - Therefore, the solubility product is 1.07 x 10<sup>-8</sup> mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the solubility of a compound from its solubility product**
> 
> Calculate the solubility of a saturated solution of copper(II) oxide, CuO, with a solubility product of 5.9 x 10<sup>-36</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Write down the equilibrium equation:
> 
> **CuO (s) ⇌ Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + O**<sup>**2-**</sup>** (aq)**
> 
> - **Step 2: **Write down the equilibrium expression:
> 
> ***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** = [Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)] [O**<sup>**2-**</sup>** (aq)]**
> 
> - **Step 3: **Simplify the equilibrium expression:
> 
>   - The ratio of Cu<sup>2+</sup> to O<sup>2-</sup> is 1:1
>   - [Cu<sup>2+</sup>(aq)] = [O<sup>2-</sup>(aq)] so the expression can be simplified to:
> 
> ***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** = [Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)]**<sup>**2**</sup>
> 
> - **Step 4: **Substitute the value of *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> into the expression to find the concentration:
> 
> **5.9 x 10**<sup>**-36**</sup>** = [Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)]**<sup>**2**</sup>
> 
> **[Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)] = **$\sqrt{5.9\times10^{-36}}$
> 
> **[Cu**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)] = 2.4 x 10**<sup>**-18**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>
> 
> - Since [CuO (s)] = [Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq)], the solubility of copper oxide is 2.4 x 10<sup>-18</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **Exam Hint**
> Remember that the solubility product is only applicable to very slightly soluble salts and cannot be used for soluble salts such as:
> 
> - Group 1 element salts
> - All nitrate salts
> - All ammonium salts
> - Many sulfate salts
> - Many halide salts (except for lead(II) halides and silver halides)

bodyMd:
# Solubility Product

## The Solubility Product, Ksp

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_phqcyxJvJchDcTMN`

## The Solubility Product, Ksp

- **Solubility **is defined as the **number of grams **or **moles **of compound needed to **saturate **100 g of **water**, or it can also be defined in terms of 1 kg of water, at a given temperature

  - For example, sodium chloride (NaCl) is considered to be a **soluble **salt as a saturated solution contains 36 g of NaCl per 100 g of water
  - Lead chloride (PbCl<sub>2</sub>) on the other hand is an **insoluble **salt as a saturated solution only contains 0.99 g of PbCl<sub>2</sub> per 100 g of water

### Solubility product

- The **solubility product **(***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>) is:

  - The product of the concentrations of each ion in a saturated solution of a relatively soluble salt
  - At 298 K
  - Raised to the power of their relative concentrations

**C (s) ⇌ aA**<sup>**x+**</sup>** (aq) + bB**<sup>**y-**</sup>** (aq)**

***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>*** *****= [A**<sup>**x+**</sup>** (aq)]**<sup>**a**</sup>** [B**<sup>**y-**</sup>** (aq)]**<sup>**b**</sup>

- When an **undissolved ionic compound** is in contact with a **saturated solution of its ions**, an equilibrium is established
- The ions move from the solid to the saturated solution at the same rate as they move from the solution to the solid

  - For example, the undissolved magnesium chloride (MgCl<sub>2</sub>) is in equilibrium with a saturated solution of its ions

**MgCl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (s) ⇌ Mg**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + 2Cl**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**

#### Ions in a saturated solution

![Diagram showing dynamic equilibrium of MgCl2 solution. Arrows indicate ion exchange between undissolved salt layer and saturated solution.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/33fa1e07f6b7-15771-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads20250614209.png)

*When the undissolved magnesium chloride salt comes in contact with its ions in a saturated solution, an equilibrium between the salt and ions is established*

- The **solubility product **for this equilibrium is:

***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>*** =***** [Mg**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)] [Cl**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)]**<sup>**2**</sup>

- The *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> is only useful for **sparingly soluble salts**
- The smaller the value of *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>, the lower the solubility of the salt

## Ksp Expressions

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_y57yCcdf7wxdpZr9`

## Ksp Expressions

- The general equilibrium expression for the **solubility product** (*K*<sub>*sp*</sub>) is:

**C (s) ⇌ aA**<sup>**x+**</sup>** (aq) + bB**<sup>**y-**</sup>** (aq)**

***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>*** *****= [A**<sup>**x+**</sup>** (aq)]**<sup>**a**</sup>** [B**<sup>**y-**</sup>** (aq)]**<sup>**b**</sup>

> **Worked Example**
> **Expressing *****K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** of ionic compounds**
> 
> - Give the equilibrium expressions, including units, for the solubility products of the following ionic compounds:
> 
>   1. Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>
>   2. Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>
>   3. SnCO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> **Answer 1 - Ca(OH)**<sub>**2**</sub>**:**
> 
> - **Step 1** - Write the balanced chemical equation:
> 
> Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) $\rightleftharpoons$ Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)
> 
> - **Step 2** - Write the *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>* *expression:
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] [OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup>
> 
> - **Step 3 **- Deduce the units:
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>] x [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>2</sup>
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>3</sup>
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>* *= mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>
> 
> **Answer 2 - Fe**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>**:**
> 
> - **Step 1** - Write the balanced chemical equation:
> 
> Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (s) $\rightleftharpoons$ 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 3O<sup>2–</sup> (aq)
> 
> - **Step 2** - Write the *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>* *expression:
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup> [O<sup>2–</sup> (aq)]<sup>3</sup>
> 
> 1. **Step 3 **- Deduce the units:
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>2</sup> x [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>3</sup>
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>5</sup>
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>* *= mol<sup>5</sup> dm<sup>-15</sup>
> 
> **Answer 3 - SnCO**<sub>**3**</sub>**:**
> 
> - **Step 1** - Write the balanced chemical equation:
> 
> SnCO<sub>3</sub> (s) $\rightleftharpoons$ Sn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq)
> 
> - **Step 2** - Write the *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>* *expression:
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [Sn<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq)]
> 
> - **Step 3 **- Deduce the units:
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>] x [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> = [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>2</sup>
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>* *= mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

title: The Common Ion Effect
bodyMd:
# The Common Ion Effect

## The Solubility Product & the Common Ion Effect

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_mjhMDJVnvhydvMWZ`

## The Solubility Product & the Common Ion Effect

- A **saturated solution **is a solution that contains the **maximum **amount of dissolved salt
- If a second compound, which has an ion **in common **with the dissolved salt, is added to the saturated solution, the solubility of the salt reduces, and a solid **precipitate **will be formed
- This is also known as the **common ion effect**
- For example, if a solution of **potassium chloride **(KCl) is added to a **saturated solution of silver chloride** (AgCl) a precipitate of silver chloride will be formed

  - The chloride ion is the common ion
- The **solubility product** can be used to predict whether a precipitate will form or not

  - A precipitate will form if the product of the ion concentrations is **greater than** the solubility product (*K*<sub>*sp*</sub>)

### Common ion effect in silver chloride

- When a **KCl** solution is added to a saturated solution of **AgCl**, an AgCl precipitate forms
- In a **saturated** AgCl solution, the silver chloride is in equilibrium with its ions

**AgCl (s) ⇌ Ag**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + Cl**<sup>**-**</sup>** (aq)**

- When a solution of potassium chloride is added:

  - Both KCl and AgCl have the common Cl<sup>-</sup> ion
  - There is an increased Cl<sup>-</sup> concentration so the equilibrium position shifts to the left
  - The increase in Cl<sup>-</sup> concentration also means that [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] [Cl<sup>-</sup>(aq)] is **greater** than the *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> for AgCl
  - As a result, the AgCl is **precipitated**

#### The common ion effect with KCl (aq) and AgCl (aq)

![Diagram illustrating chloride ions as common ions in solutions; adding KCl to AgCl solution forms a precipitate, decreasing solubility.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/842563ffd85c-13828-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021025-5-e.png)

*The addition of potassium chloride to a saturated solution of silver chloride results in the precipitate of silver chloride*

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculations using the *****K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** values and the concentration of the common ion**
> 
> Predict whether a precipitate of CaSO<sub>4</sub> will form if a saturated solution of 1.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> CaSO<sub>4</sub> is mixed with an equal volume of 1.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
> 
> *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>* *CaSO<sub>4</sub> = 2.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Determine the equilibrium reaction of CaSO<sub>4</sub>:
> 
> **CaSO**<sub>**4**</sub>** (s) ⇌ Ca**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq) + SO**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**2-**</sup>** (aq)**
> 
> - **Step 2: **Write down the equilibrium expression for *K*<sub>*sp*</sub>:
> 
> ***K***<sub>***sp***</sub>** = [Ca**<sup>**2+**</sup>** (aq)] [SO**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**2-**</sup>** (aq)]**
> 
> - **Step 3: **Determine the concentrations of the ions:
> 
>   - There are equal volumes of each solution
>   - This means that the total solution was diluted by a factor of 2
>   - The new concentration of the Ca<sup>2+</sup> ion is **halved**:
>   
>     - [Ca<sup>2+</sup>] =  $\frac{1.0\times10^{-3}}{2}$
>     - [Ca<sup>2+</sup>] = 5.0 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
>   - The sulfate ion concentration remains the same as it is a common ion and its concentration is the same in both solutions
> 
> - **Step 4: **Substitute the values into the expression:
> 
>   - Product of the ion concentrations = [Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] x [SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)]
>   - Product of the ion concentrations = (5.0 x 10<sup>-4</sup>) x (1.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup>)
>   - Product of the ion concentrations = 5.0 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>
> 
> - **Step 5: **Determine if a precipitate will form:
> 
>   - As the product of the ion concentration (5.0 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) is smaller than the *K*<sub>*sp*</sub> value (2.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>), the CaSO<sub>4</sub> precipitate will **not** be formed

title: Partition Coefficients
bodyMd:
# Partition Coefficients

## The Partition Coefficient

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_tXywm7qJbKnHM9FS`

## The Partition Coefficient

- The **partition coefficient (*****K***<sub>***pc***</sub>**) **is the ratio of the concentrations of a **solute** in two different immiscible solvents in contact with each other when equilibrium has been established (at a particular temperature)
- For example, **methylamine (CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**NH**<sub>**2**</sub>**) **is dissolved in two immiscible solvents:

  - Water
  - An organic solvent
- A **separating funnel **is shaken with the organic solvent and aqueous methylamine
- The methylamine is **soluble **in both solvents, so when the mixture is left to settle an **equilibrium **is established

  - The **rate** of methylamine molecules moving from the organic layer into the aqueous layer is **equal** to the rate of molecules moving from the aqueous layer to the organic layer

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**NH**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(aq) ⇌ CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**NH**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(organic solvent)**

- The value of its **equilibrium constant **is also called the **partition coefficient**

***K***<sub>***pc***</sub>*** = ***$\frac{[ CH_{3} NH_{2} ( \text{organic} \text{solvent} ) ]}{[ CH_{3} NH_{2} ( \text{aq} ) ]}$

#### Defining the partition coefficient

![Separatory funnel showing organic solvent and water layers with methylamine. Partition coefficient formula, Kpc, displayed on the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/7fc5cc2ffb9d-53256-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021025-5-e.png)

*The partition coefficient is the ratio of methylamine molecules in the organic and aqueous layer once equilibrium has been established*

## Partition Coefficient Calculations

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_ZBsV3XrYB3nJbxCz`

## Partition Coefficient Calculations

- The **partition** **coefficient** (*K*<sub>*pc*</sub>) for a system in which the solute is in the same physical state in the two solvents can be calculated using the equilibrium expression

> **Worked Example**
> **Calculating the partition coefficient**
> 
> 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of a 0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of aqueous methylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) was shaken with 75.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of an organic solvent at 25 °C and left in the separating funnel to allow an equilibrium to be established.
> 
> Only 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of the aqueous layer was run off and titrated against 0.225 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> dilute hydrochloric acid (HCI) with an end-point of 14.1 cm<sup>3</sup> of HCI.
> 
> Calculate the partition coefficient of methylamine between the organic solvent and water.
> 
> **Answer**
> 
> - **Step 1: **Write down the equilibrium equation:
> 
> **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**NH**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(aq) ⇌ CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**NH**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(organic solvent)**
> 
> - **Step 2: **Write down the equilibrium expression:
> 
> ***K***<sub>***pc***</sub>*** = ***$\frac{[ CH_{3} NH_{2} ( \text{organic} \text{solvent} ) ]}{[ CH_{3} NH_{2} ( \text{aq} ) ]}$
> 
> - **Step 3: **Determine how many moles of CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> have reacted with HCl at the end-point:
> 
>   - At the **end-point,** all CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq) has been neutralised by HCl (aq)
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq) + HCl (aq) → CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>Cl (aq)
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> and HCl react in a ratio of 1:1
> 
> Mol (HCl) = mol (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) = 0.225 x 0.0141
> 
> Mol (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) = 3.1725 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> - **Step 4: **Determine the number of moles of CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> present in the aqueous layer:
> 
>   - Only 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of the aqueous layer was used to titrate against HCl
>   - Thus, 3.1725 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol of CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> was present in only 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of the aqueous layer
>   - The number of moles of CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> in 100 cm<sup>3 </sup>**aqueous layer **is, therefore:
> 
> Mol (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> aqueous layer) = 3.1725 x 10<sup>-3</sup> x 2 = 6.345 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> - **Step 5: **Determine the number of moles of CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> in the organic layer:
> 
> Mol CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic layer) = mol CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2 </sub>(total) - mol CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2 </sub>(aqueous layer)
> 
> Mol CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (total) = 0.100 x 0.150 = 0.015 mol
> 
> Mol CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic layer) = 0.015 - 6.345 x 10<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> Mol CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic layer) = 8.655 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> - **Step 6: **Change the number of moles into **concentrations:**
> 
>   - Aqueous layer:
> 
> Concentration (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> in aqueous layer) = $\frac{6.345\times10^{-3}}{0.100}$
> 
> Concentration (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> in aqueous layer) = 0.06345 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> - Organic layer:
> 
> Concentration (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> in organic layer) = $\frac{8.655\times10^{-3}}{0.075}$
> 
> Concentration (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> in organic layer) = 0.1154 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> - **Step 7: **Substitute the values into the *K*<sub>*pc*</sub> expression:
> 
> *K*<sub>*pc*</sub> *=* $\frac{0.1154}{0.06345}$
> 
> *K*<sub>*pc*</sub>*=* 1.82
> 
> - Since the value of *K*<sub>*pc*</sub> is **larger than 1**, methylamine is more soluble in the organic solvent than in water

## Factors Affecting the Partition Coefficient

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_TP6qxp9zNWzKKzHR`

## Factors Affecting the Partition Coefficient

- The partition coefficient (*K*<sub>*pc*</sub>*)* depends on the **solubilities **of the **solute **in the two **solvents**
- The degree of solubility of a solute is determined by how strong the **intermolecular bonds **between **solute** and **solvent**  are
- The strength of these intermolecular bonds, in turn, depends on the **polarity **of the **solute **and **solvent molecules**
- For example, ammonia is more soluble in water than in an organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride (CCl<sub>4</sub>)

  - Ammonia and water are both polar molecules that form **hydrogen bonds **with each other
  - Ammonia forms **permanent dipole-induced dipole **forces with the non-polar CCl<sub>4</sub> molecules
  - Since these forces are **much** weaker than hydrogen bonding, ammonia is **less soluble **in CCl<sub>4</sub>
- When *K*<sub>*pc*</sub> is < 1 the **solute **is more soluble in water than the organic solvent
- When *K*<sub>*pc*</sub> is > 1 the **solute **is more soluble in the organic solvent than the water

title: Chemical Kinetics Calculations

# Chemical Kinetics Calculations

## Chemical Kinetics Calculations

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_SbTsrshCdzPGYxtC`

## Chemical Kinetics Calculations

### Order of reaction

- The **order of reaction **shows how the concentration of a reactant affects the rate of reaction

**Rate = *****k***** [A]**<sup>**m**</sup>** [B]**<sup>**n**</sup>

- When m or n is zero = the concentration of the reactants does not affect the rate
- When **the order of reaction** (m or n) of a reactant is 0, its concentration is ignored
- The **overall order of reaction** is the sum of the powers of the reactants in a rate equation
- For example, in the reaction below, the overall order of reaction is 2 (1 + 1)

**Rate = *****k***** [NO**<sub>**2**</sub>**] [Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>**]**

### Order of reaction from concentration-time graphs

- In a** zero-order **reaction, the concentration of the reactant decreases linearly with time

  - The graph is a **straight line with a negative gradient**

#### A zero-order concentration-time graph

![Graph showing a red line with a negative slope, depicting decreasing reactant concentration (mol/dm³) over time (s). Axes are labelled.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/cbfa92b3666b-54847-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-6-r.png)

*A zero-order concentration-time graph is a straight line*

- In a **first-order **reaction, the concentration of the reactant decreases with time

  - The graph is a curve going downwards and eventually plateaus

#### A first-order concentration-time graph

![Graph showing a red curve decreasing over time, with axes labelled "Concentration of Reactant (mol dm⁻³)" and "Time (s)".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/5a813273e900-35604-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-6-r.png)

*A first-order concentration-time graph is a smooth curve*

- In a **second-order** reaction, the concentration of the reactant decreases more steeply with time

  - The concentration of reactant decreases **more** with increasing time compared to in a first-order reaction
  - The graph is a steeper curve going downwards

#### A second-order concentration-time graph

![Graph showing a red curve with concentration of reactant (mol/dm³) decreasing over time (seconds), forming a downward slope.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/98d38ef56727-35183-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-6-r.png)

*A second-order concentration-time graph is a smooth and steep curve*

#### Order of reaction from initial rate

- The **progress** of the reaction can be followed by measuring the **initial** **rates** of the reaction using various **initial concentrations **of each reactant
- These rates can then be plotted against concentration in a rate-concentration graph
- In a** zero-order **reaction, the rate doesn’t depend on the concentration of the reactant

  - The rate of the reaction therefore remains constant throughout the reaction
  - The graph is a **horizontal line**
  - The rate equation is **rate = *****k***

#### A zero-order rate-concentration graph

![Graph showing a constant reaction rate on the y-axis against varying concentration of reactant on the x-axis, with a horizontal line.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/21b386a834fd-58156-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-6-r.png)

*A zero-order rate-concentration graph is a flat line*

- In a **first-order **reaction, the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of a reactant

  - The rate of the reaction decreases as the concentration of the reactant decreases when it gets used up during the reaction
  - The graph is a **straight line**
  - The rate equation is **rate = *****k***** [A]**

#### A first-order rate-concentration graph

![Graph showing reaction rate versus reactant concentration. The red line indicates a direct proportionality, with axes labelled in molarity units.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/8cf71858c738-58855-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-6-r.png)

*A first-order rate-concentration graph is a straight line with a fixed gradient, k*

- In a **second-order** reaction, the rate is directly proportional to the square of concentration of a reactant

  - The rate of the reaction decreases more as the concentration of the reactant decreases when it gets used up during the reaction
  - The graph is a **curved line**
  - The rate equation is **rate = *****k***** [A]**<sup>**2**</sup>

#### A second-order rate-concentration graph

![Graph shows a curved line increasing from the origin, depicting reaction rate vs. reactant concentration. Axes labelled in mol dm⁻³ and mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/bad6744d2a64-38930-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-6-r.png)

*A second-order rate-concentration graph is a smooth curve*

### Order of reaction from half-life

- The order of a reaction can also be deduced from its **half-life (t**<sub>**1/2 **</sub>**)**
- For a **zero-order **reaction, the successive half-lives decrease with time

  - This means that it would take **less** time for the concentration of reactant to halve as the reaction progresses
- The half-life of a **first-order **reaction remains **constant **throughout the reaction

  - The amount of time required for the concentration of reactants to halve will be the same during the entire reaction
- For a **second-order **reaction, the half-life increases with time

  - This means that as the reaction is taking place, it takes more time for the concentration of reactants to halve

#### Half-lives of zero, first and second-order reactions

![Three graphs showing reaction orders: zero order (linear decline), first order (exponential decay), and second order (steeper exponential decay).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/537967988ba8-56892-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-6-r.png)

*Zero-order reactions have a decreasing half-life, first-order reactions have a constant half-life and second-order reactions have an increasing half-life *

### Calculating the initial rate

- The **initial rate **can be calculated by using the **initial concentrations **of the reactants in the rate equation
- For example, in the reaction of bromomethane (CH<sub>3</sub>Br) with hydroxide (OH<sup>-</sup>) ions to form methanol (CH<sub>3</sub>OH):

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**Br + OH**<sup>**-**</sup>** → CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**OH + Br**<sup>**-**</sup>** **

- The rate **equation** is:

**Rate = *****k***** [CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**Br] [OH**<sup>**-**</sup>**]**

- Where *k* = 1.75 x 10<sup>-2</sup> dm<sup>-2</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>
- If the **initial concentrations **of CH<sub>3</sub>Br and OH<sup>-</sup> are 0.0200 and 0.0100 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> respectively, the **initial rate** of reaction is:

  - Rate = *k* [CH<sub>3</sub>Br] [OH<sup>-</sup>]
  - Initial rate = 1.75 x 10<sup>-2</sup> x (0.0200) x (0.0100)
  - Initial rate = 3.50 x 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>

### Calculating Units

- When you are asked to calculate the rate constant, *k*, for a reaction you must also be able to deduce the units
- This is done by replacing the values in the rearranged rate equation with the units of that value
- The units can then be combined or cancelled as required
- For example, to calculate the units for the above reaction:

![Units of k calculation showing division of mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ by mol dm⁻³ squared, simplifying to s⁻¹ over mol dm⁻³, resulting in mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/35b966fd8c35-20766-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021095-2-3.png)

title: Chemical Kinetics Terminology
bodyMd:
# Chemical Kinetics Terminology ## Chemical Kinetics Terminology > **Spec point** — `spcpt_pfYRwf4P7YjvWkPb` ## Chemical Kinetics Terminology - The **rate of reaction **refers to the change in the amount or concentration of a reactant or product per unit time and can be found by: - Measuring the **decrease in the concentration of a reactant **OR - Measuring the **increase in the concentration of a product** over **time** - The units of rate of reaction are mol dm-3 s-1 $\mathrm{Rate} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{reaction}=\frac{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{concentration}}{\mathrm{time}}$ ### Rate equation - Rate equations can **only** be determined **experimentally** - They cannot be found from the **stoichiometric equations** - For the general reaction of P and Q reacting together to form products: **P (aq) + Q (aq) → R (aq) + S (g)** - The rate equation will include: - A rate / proportionality constant, *k* - This can be calculated from the gradient of the graph - The concentration of the reactants - They are shown in square brackets for concentration, e.g. [P] and [Q] - The order to which each reactant is raised - They are shown as powers, e.g. m and n - The order with respect to any reactant can **only **be 0, 1 or 2 **Rate of reaction = *****k***** [P]****m**** [Q]****n** - The rate equation does not include the concentration of the products - This is because they do not affect the rate of reaction ### Example reactions for rate equations - The following general reaction will be used as an example to study the rate of reaction **D (aq) → E (aq) + F (g) ** - The rate of reaction at different concentrations of D is measured and tabulated #### Rate of reactions table | **[D] (mol dm****-3****)** | **Rate (mol dm****-3**** s****-1****)** | $\frac{rate}{[ D ]}$** (s****-1****)** | |---|---|---| | 3.00 | 2.00 x 10-3 | 6.67 x 10-4 | | 2.00 | 1.33 x 10-3 | 6.67 x 10-4 | | 1.00 | 6.60 x 10-4 | 6.67 x 10-4 | - A **directly proportional **relationship between the **rate** of the reaction and the **concentration** of D is observed when a graph is plotted ![Graph showing the rate versus concentration [D]. Line passes through points (1,1), (2,2), and (3,2). Gradient calculation equals 6.67 x 10⁻⁴.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/feb0f4bf169d-32393-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021105-2-1.png) *Rate of reaction over various concentrations of D* - For the above reaction, the rate equation is: **Rate = *****k***** [D]** - The value of the rate / proportionality constant, *k*, can be calculated from the results or from two points on the graph - For this example, the value is is 6.67 x 10-4 s-1 #### Nitric oxide and hydrogen - The reaction between nitric oxide and hydrogen is: **2NO (g) + 2H****2**** (g) → N****2**** (g) + 2H****2****O (g)** - The experimentally determined **rate equation **for this reaction is: **rate = *****k***** [NO]****2**** [H****2****]** - By keeping the concentration of one reactant constant, the rate equation can show the effect of each reactants - Keeping [H2] constant: **Rate = *****k*****1**** [NO]****2** - This means that the effect of [H2] is fixed - Any change in the rate of reaction is caused by [NO] - The change in the rate of reaction is **proportional to** **the** **square** of [NO]: - Keeping [NO] constant: **Rate = *****k*****2**** [H****2****]** - This means that effect of [NO] is fixed - Any change in the rate of reaction is caused by [H2] - The change in the rate of reaction is **proportional **to [H2]: - Both sets of experiments show different parts of the same **overall rate equation:** **Rate = *****k***** [NO]****2**** [H****2****]** - Notice that the [H2] does not have an order of 2 - This is because the order must be determined experimentally, not from the equation ### Order of reaction - The **order **of a reactant shows how the concentration of a reactant affects the rate of reaction - It is the power to which the concentration of that reactant is raised in the rate equation - The order can be 0, 1 or 2 - When the order of reaction with respect to a chemical is 0 - Changing the concentration of the chemical has no effect on the rate of the reaction - Therefore, it is not included in the rate equation - When the order of reaction with respect to a chemical is 1 - The concentration of the chemical is directly proportional to the rate of reaction, e.g. doubling the concentration of the chemical doubles the rate of reaction - The chemical is included in the rate equation - When the order of reaction with respect to a chemical is 2 - The rate is directly proportional to the square of the concentration of that chemical, e.g. doubling the concentration of the chemical increases the rate of reaction by a factor of four - The chemical is included in the rate equation (appearing as a squared term) - The **overall order of reaction** is the sum of the powers of the reactants in a rate equation **Rate = *****k***** [NO]****2 ****[H****2****]** - For example, in the rate equation above, the reaction is: - Second-order with respect to NO - First-order with respect to H2 - Third-order overall (2 + 1) > **Worked Example** > The chemical equation for the thermal decomposition of dinitrogen pentoxide is: > > 2N2O5 (g)** → **4NO2 (g) + O2 (g) > > The rate equation for this reaction is: > > Rate = *k*[N2O5 (g)] > > 1. State the order of the reaction with respect to dinitrogen pentoxide > 2. Deduce the effect on the rate of reaction if the concentration of dinitrogen pentoxide is tripled > > **Final answer:** **Answers:** > > 1. The order with respect to dinitrogen pentoxide: > > - Dinitrogen pentoxide features in the rate equation, therefore, it cannot be order zero / 0 > - The dinitrogen pentoxide is not raised to a power, which means that it cannot be order 2 / second order > - Therefore, the order with respect to dinitrogen pentoxide must be **order 1 / first order** > 2. The effect of tripling [N2O5]: > > - Since the reaction is first order, the concentration of dinitrogen pentoxide is directly proportional to the rate > - This means that if the concentration of the dinitrogen pentoxide is tripled, then the rate of reaction will also **triple** ## Deducing Orders - To derive the rate equation for a reaction, you can use a graph or a table of results - The type and shape of the graph indicates the order with respect to a reactant - A table or results requires calculation - Take the reactants one at a time and find the order with respect to each reactant individually - Steps to derive a rate equation: 1. Identify two experiments where: - The concentration of one reactant changes and the concentrations of all other reactants remain constant - Calculate what has happened to the concentration of the reactant - Calculate what has happened to the rate of reaction - Determine the order with respect to that reactant 2. Repeat this for all of the reactants - Work methodically through each reactant, one at a time - Determine the order with respect to all reactants > **Worked Example** > Use the information in the table to determine the rate equation for the nucleophilic substitution of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane by hydroxide ions: > > **(CH****3****)****3****CBr + OH****-**** → (CH****3****)****3****COH + Br****-** > > **Table to show the experimental data of the above reaction** > > | **Experiment** | **Initial [(CH****3****)****3****CBr]**
**/ mol dm****-3**** ** | **Initial [OH****–****]**
**/ mol dm****-3**** ** | **Initial rate of reaction**
**/ mol dm****-3**** s****-1** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **1** | 1.0 x 10-3 | 2.0 x 10-3 | 3.0 x 10-3 | > | **2** | 2.0 x 10-3 | 2.0 x 10-3 | 6.0 x 10-3 | > | **3** | 1.0 x 10-3 | 4.0 x 10-3 | 1.2 x 10-2 | > > **Final answer:** **Answer:** > > **Order with respect to [(CH****3****)****3****CBr]:** > > - Using experiments 1 and 2: > > - The [OH-] has remained constant > - The [(CH3)3CBr] has doubled > - The rate of the reaction has also doubled > - Therefore, the order with respect to [(CH3)3CBr] is 1 (first order) > > **Order with respect to [OH****-****]:** > > - Using experiments 1 and 3: > > - The [(CH3)3CBr] has remained constant > - The [OH-] has doubled > - The rate of reaction has increased by a factor of 4 (i.e. increased by 22) > - Therefore, the order with respect to [OH-] is 2 (second order) > > **Building the rate equation:** > > - Once you know the order with respect to all of the reactants, you put them together to form the rate equation > > - If a reactant is order 0, it should not appear in the rate equation > - If a reactant is order 1, then it features in the rate equation > > - There is no need to include the number 1 as a power > - If a reactant is order 2, then it features in the rate equation with the number 2 as a power > - For this reaction, the rate equation will be: > > **Rate = k [(CH****3****)****3****CBr] [OH****-****]****2** ### Half-life - The **half-life (*****t******1/2*****) **is the time taken for the concentration of a **limiting reactant** to become half of its initial value ### Rate-determining step & intermediates - The **rate-determining step **is the slowest step in a reaction - If a reactant appears in the **rate-determining step**, then the concentration of that reactant will also appear in the **rate equation** - For example, the rate equation for the reaction below is **rate **= *k* [CH3Br] [OH–] **CH****3****Br + OH****–**** → CH****3****OH + Br****–** - This suggests that **both **CH3Br and OH– take part in the **slow rate-determining step** - This reaction is, therefore, a **bimolecular reaction** - **Unimolecular**: one species involved in the rate-determining step - **Bimolecular**: two species involved in the rate-determining step - The **intermediate** is derived from substances that react together to form it in the rate-determining step - For example, for the reaction above the intermediate would consist of CH3Br and OH– #### The intermediate formed during the reaction of CH3Br and hydroxide ions ![Chemical structure of bromomethanol, showing a central carbon bonded to hydrogen, hydroxyl (OH), and bromine (Br) atoms, with 3D bond lines.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/bb64895a6ebf-48799-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021015-6-r.png) *The intermediate is formed from the species that are involved in the rate-determining step (and thus appear in the rate equation)*

title: Factors affecting Rate Constant
bodyMd:
# Factors affecting Rate Constant

## Effect of Temperature on the Rate Constant

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_tdDd42XcBrjsNCKg`

## Effect of Temperature on the Rate Constant

- At higher temperatures, a greater proportion of molecules have energy greater than the activation energy
- Since the **rate constant **and **rate of reaction **are **directly proportional **to the fraction of molecules with energy equal or greater than the activation energy, then at higher temperatures:

  - The **rate constant** increases
  - The **rate of reaction** increases
- The relationship between the rate constant and the temperature is given by the following equation:

$\mathrm{ln}k=\mathrm{ln}A-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}$

- Where:

  - **ln *****k*** = natural logarithm of the rate constant
  - ***A*** = constant related to the collision frequency and orientation of the molecules
  - ***E***<sub>***a***</sub>** **= activation energy (joules, J)
  - ***R*** = gas constant (8.31 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>)
  - ***T*** = temperature (kelvin, K)
- ***A*** varies only a little bit with temperature, it can be considered a constant
- ***E***<sub>***a***</sub> and ***R*** are also constants

- A graph of ln *k* against $\frac{1}{T}$ gives a line with an equation of the form y = mx + c

$\mathrm{ln}k=\frac{-E_{a}}{R}\frac{1}{T}+\mathrm{ln}A$

- Where:

  - y = ln *k*
  - x = $\frac{1}{T}$
  - m = $\frac{-E_{a}}{R}$ (the gradient)
  - c = ln *A* (the y-intercept)

- The equation shows that an **increase **in temperature (higher value of *T*) gives a **greater **value of ln *k* (and therefore a higher value of *k*)
- Since the **rate of the reaction **depends on the **rate constant **(*k*) an increase in *k* also means an increased rate of reaction

#### Example graph of ln k over 1/T

![Graph with ln k vs. 1/T (K⁻¹), showing a red line of best fit. Gradient is -Ea/R and intercept is ln A. Grid background with labelled axes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/4062ff6df749-53908-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2022015-2-5.png)

*The graph of ln k over 1/T is a straight line with gradient -Ea/R*

> **Exam Hint**
> You are not required to learn this equation however it is helpful in understanding the effects of temperature on the rate constant.

title: Half-Life
bodyMd:
# Half-Life

## First Order Reaction Half-life

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_qrns7rFJ3XYbdN3M`

## First Order Reaction Half-life

- The **half-life** of a **first-order** reaction is **independent **of the concentration of reactants

  - This means that despite the **concentrations of the reactants decreasing **during the reaction
  - The amount of time taken for the **concentrations of the reactants to halve** will remain the same throughout the reaction
  - The concentration-time graph for a first-order reaction is a downward curve with a constant half-life.
- The **rearrangement** of the **methyl group **(CH<sub>3</sub>) in ethanenitrile (CH<sub>3</sub>CN) is an example of a first-order reaction with rate equation **rate = *****k***** [CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CN]**

#### Rearrangement of the CH<sub>3</sub> group in CH<sub>3</sub>CN

![Reaction Kinetics - Rearrangement of Methyl Group, downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/faaf86b3c8d3-5-6-reaction-kinetics-rearrangement-of-methyl-gr.png)

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CN (g) → CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**NC (g)**

- Experimental data on the changes in concentration over time suggests that the **half-life** is constant

  - Even if the half-lives are slightly different from each other, they can still be considered to remain constant
- This means that no matter what the original concentration of the CH<sub>3</sub>CN is, the half-life will always be around 10.0 minutes

#### Half-life table

|---|---|
| 8.00 - 4.00 | 10.0 |
| 4.00 - 2.00 | 9.50 |
| 2.00 - 1.00 | 9.25 |

*Since this is a first-order reaction, the time taken for the concentration to halve remains constant*

# Multi-Step Reactions

## Kinetics of Multi-Step Reactions

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_7CpJ4YCHWydphVQr`

## Kinetics of Multi-Step Reactions

- The **reaction** **mechanism** of a reaction describes how many steps are involved in the **making **and **breaking** of bonds during a chemical reaction
- It is the slowest step in a reaction and includes the reactants that have an impact on the reaction rate when their concentrations are changed

  - Therefore, all reactants that appear in the **rate equation **will also appear in the rate-determining step
  - This means that zero-order reactants and **intermediates **will not be present in the rate-determining step

### Predicting the reaction mechanism

- The **overall reaction equation** and **rate equation** can be used to predict a possible reaction mechanism of a reaction
- For example, nitrogen dioxide (NO<sub>2</sub>) and carbon monoxide (CO) react to form nitrogen monoxide (NO) and carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>)
- The overall reaction equation is:

**NO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + CO (g) → NO (g) + CO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)**

- The rate equation is:

**Rate = *****k***** [NO**<sub>**2**</sub>**]**<sup>**2**</sup>

- From the rate equation, it can be concluded that the reaction is **zero order** with respect to CO (g) and **second order** with respect to NO<sub>2</sub> (g)
- This means that there are **two molecules** of NO<sub>2</sub> (g) involved in the **rate-determining step**
- A possible reaction mechanism could therefore be:

  - **Step 1:**
  
    - **2NO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) → NO (g) + NO**<sub>**3**</sub>** (g)**     **slow **(rate-determining step)
  - **Step 2:**
  
    - **NO**<sub>**3**</sub>** (g) + CO (g) → NO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + CO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)**     **fast**
  - **Overall:**
  
    - **2****NO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + ****NO**<sub>**3**</sub>** (g)**** + CO (g) → NO (g) + ****NO**<sub>**3**</sub>** (g)**** + ****NO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) ****+ CO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)**
    - Which simplifies to** NO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + CO (g) → NO (g) + CO**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g)**

### Predicting the reaction order & deducing the rate equation

- The **order** of a reactant and thus the rate equation can be deduced from a reaction mechanism given that the rate-determining step is known
- For example, the reaction of nitrogen oxide (NO) with hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>) to form nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>) and water

**2NO (g) + 2H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) → N**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + 2H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)**

- The reaction mechanism for this reaction is:

  - **Step 1:**
  
    - **NO (g) + NO (g) → N**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g)**     **fast**
  - **Step 2:**
  
    - **N**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) → H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) + N**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (g) **    **slow **(rate-determining step)
  - **Step 3:**
  
    - **N**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) → N**<sub>**2**</sub>** (g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)     fast**
  - The second step in this reaction mechanism is the **rate-determining step**
  - The rate-determining step consists of:
  
    - N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> which is formed from the reaction of **two NO molecules**
    - **One H**<sub>**2**</sub>** molecule**
- The reaction is, therefore, **second order **with respect to NO and **first order **with respect to H<sub>2</sub>

  - So, the **rate** **equation** becomes:

**Rate = *****k***** [NO]**<sup>**2**</sup>** [H**<sub>**2**</sub>**]**

- The reaction is, therefore, **third-order overall**

### Identifying the rate-determining step

- The rate-determining step can be identified from a rate equation given that the reaction mechanism is known
- For example, propane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) undergoes bromination under alkaline solutions
- The overall reaction is:

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** + Br**<sub>**2**</sub>** + OH**<sup>**-**</sup>** → CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**Br + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O + Br**<sup>**-**</sup>

- The reaction mechanism is:

![Chemical reaction mechanism showing propane reacting slowly with hydroxide to form an intermediate, then rapidly with bromine to form 1-bromopropane.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/dbe470b93009-56239-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021025-6-r.png)

*Reaction mechanism of the bromination of propane under alkaline conditions*

- The rate equation is:

**Rate = *****k***** [CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**] [OH**<sup>**-**</sup>**]**

- From the rate equation, it can be deduced that only CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> and OH<sup>- </sup>are involved in the **rate-determining step** and not bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>)
- CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> and OH<sup>-</sup> are only involved in step 1

  - Therefore, the **rate-determining step **is step 1 of the reaction mechanism

### Identifying intermediates & catalyst

- When a rate equation includes a species that is not part of the chemical reaction equation then this species is a **catalyst**
- For example, the halogenation of butanone under acidic conditions
- The reaction mechanism is:

**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**COCH**<sub>**3**</sub>** + I**<sub>**2**</sub>** **$\overset{H^{+}}{\rightarrow}$** CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**COCH**<sub>**2**</sub>**I + HI**

- The reaction mechanism is:

![Four-step reaction mechanism with molecular structures: Step 1 fast equilibrium, Step 2 slow, Step 3 fast, Step 4 fast equilibrium with iodine.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/3616afaf45c6-55514-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2022015-6-r.png)

*Reaction mechanism of the halogenation of butanone under acidic conditions*

The rate equation is:

**Rate = *****k***** [CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**COCH**<sub>**3**</sub>**] [H**<sup>**+**</sup>**]**

- The H<sup>+</sup> is not present in the **chemical reaction equation** but **does **appear in the rate equation

  - H<sup>+</sup> must therefore be a **catalyst**
- Furthermore, the rate equation suggests that CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> and H<sup>+</sup> must be involved in the rate-determining (slowest) step
- The CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> and H<sup>+</sup> appear in the rate-determining step in the form of an **intermediate **(which is a combination of the two species)

#### The intermediate formed in the reaction of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> and H<sup>+</sup>

![Chemical reaction showing a ketone (CH3CH2C(CH3)=O) reacting with H+ to form an intermediate with a hydroxyl group; labelled "INTERMEDIATE".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/1a5c37bcecf379cd98e83aa74aa9472920092428/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/assets/576768012047-1928-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021025-6-re.png)

*This intermediate is formed in the rate-determining step*
